utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Korner, are you ready to open?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If I can find a microphone. Your Honours, I am ready to open. Does Your Honours -- do Your Honours wish to hear who is appearing before I open, or do you want me to go straight into opening?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do Your Honours want me to introduce who is sitting here and appearing for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then I'm perfectly happy to go into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, appearing for the Office of the Prosecutor today I'm going from my left to right, Crispian Smith, case manager in this case; Belinda Pidwell, lawyer in this case; to my right Thomas Hannis, lawyer; and Matthew Olmsted, lawyer in this case; and myself, Joanna Korner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing for Mr. Stanisic's Defence, myself, Mr. Slobodan Zecevic, Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Mr. Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Tatjana Savic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Zupljanin's Defence, I'm Igor Pantelic, lead counsel. Next to me is my co-counsel, Mr. Dragan Krkovic. Left to my side is Mr. Brent Hicks, Defence counsel from Florida Bar. And next to him is Mr. Eric Tully, our case manager. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before we proceed further, I would wish to inquire of the accused separately whether they can understand the proceedings -- what we have said so far. THE ACCUSED STANISIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. THE ACCUSED ZUPLJANIN: [Interpretation] I can understand as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the case which you are about to hear over the next few months concentrates on the role of the Bosnian Serb police during the conflict, which took place in 1992 in Bosnia-Herzegovina and of course continued longer. The indictment, in this case, as you are aware, deals with those events of 1992. The Bosnian Serb police, in short form the RS MUP, I will explain in a moment or two what MUP stands for. RS, of course, is Republika Srpska. The name Republika Srpska did not come into existence until later on in 1992, but it's just easier throughout if one talks about the RS MUP. The two accused in this case, Mico Stanisic, as minister of the interior of what became known as Republika Srpska, and Stojan Zupljanin as chief of the security services centre, otherwise called CSB, in the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, represent the highest level of the RS MUP and the regional level. The events of 1992, as have already been well-documented in previous cases before this Tribunal, reveal, the Prosecution say, a widespread and systematic campaign of criminal activities by the Bosnian Serbs against their fellow Bosnians who were of Muslim and Croat ethnicity or nationality, and in particular against the former, the Muslims. And when I say Bosnian Serbs, I mean those Bosnian Serbs who were the leadership of the SDS and who took part in the creation of the Bosnian Serb state and then carried out the planned activities. The criminal activities range from discriminatory measures, for example, denial of employment, restriction of movement of the lowest to mass killings at the highest, and the Prosecution say that these crimes did not take place spontaneously or by happenstance. The similarity of events which occurred in the municipalities all over Bosnia and Herzegovina, if nothing else, shows that the crimes were intended and came about as the result of a criminal enterprise. We submit that the evidence will show in this case that the criminal enterprise was planned and put into execution by the Bosnian Serb leaders in politics, the police, and the military. The objective of this plan was to remove permanently the non-Serbs from the territory which the Bosnian Serbs consider belonged, and I use that word in inverted commas because it was a word that was used by one of the leaders, which the Bosnian Serbs considered belonged to them and therefore should form part of the Serbian state within Bosnia. The participation of the MUP in this enterprise, the RS MUP, as a matter of common sense, if nothing else, was clearly integral to its success. The crimes which were envisaged and executed, if nothing else, should have been investigated and those responsible charged and prosecuted. This, as we will show, did not happen. Whilst for some of the most notorious crimes public announcements of an investigation were made, in reality these were sham investigations. Furthermore, in many of the crimes which are listed in the schedules to this indictment, members of the RS MUP were active participants therein. In general terms they participated in the original seizure of power by the Bosnian Serb leaders in most if not all of the municipalities about which evidence will be heard in this case. They were wholly or partly responsible for some of the mass killings. For example, those which occurred on Mount Vlasic or outside the medical centre in Kotor Varos. They were operating notorious camps such as Omarska and Keraterm in the Prijedor municipality. It is not suggested that every police officer, every member of the MUP took part in crimes. Some of those in positions of responsibility who took part in the activities which preceded the official establishment of the RS MUP carried out their duties in a proper professional manner. Others resigned or found themselves positions which took them out of the mainstream of the activities of the MUP. For example, taking charge of security in the Villa Bosanska in Belgrade which was used for meetings by high-ranking Bosnian Serb officials and their counterparts in Serbia proper. There was, as the evidence will show, close co-operation between the MUPs in Serbia and in Bosnian Serb territory, as well as between government figures. We should further make it clear straightaway it is not suggested that either of the two accused personally committed any murders or beatings or took part personally in looting; however, they were aware of these crimes. The evidence shows that their failure to take any action, either to investigate crimes which had taken place or take steps to prevent future crimes, was not simply a failure to act but a positive affirmation of their adherence to and participation in the criminal enterprise which was designed to rid the designated territory of its non-Serb peoples. The description of the evidence which you are about to hear in this opening is no more than a summary of the salient parts. It would be impossible to deal in any opening with every area of evidence, let alone every piece of evidence, and the intention of this opening is to set out the framework into which the evidence you will hear and assess fits. So may I start straightaway with a brief biography of the accused. First of all, Mico Stanisic, who you will see on your screens, not as he is now but as he was filmed in 1992. He's now aged 55, being born on the 30th of June, 1954. He attended the police school in Sarajevo and joined the Bosnian police force, the Bosnia-Herzegovina police force, then known as the SUP - as I say, I'll come on to explain some of these expressions - in 1973. May I just interrupt. We're going to show the video from which this clip is taken, so -- at a later stage. He then took a law degree at Sarajevo University, graduating in 1982, and in 1984 he left the police to go into business. In 1991, he returned to the Bosnian police and in May of that year was appointed secretary to the public security station, the Secretariat for Internal Affairs in Sarajevo, a position of some importance. By then, the minister of the interior was Alija Delimustafic. And in February 1992, he was appointed advisor to the minister on state security, which in the light of what was happening in February of 1992 was a touch ironic. He was a member of the SDS party at a very early stage and was on the Main Board in 1990. And if you look there, document, you will see at number 13 -- 19, Mico Stanisic. Can we just look at the title, it says: "Main Committee of the Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina," known as the SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, when was this appointment made?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The appointment, which appointment, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: His appointment to the Main Committee.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't know when it was actually made, but that document is 1990, so it must have been very early on because the parties were established sometime before the elections in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But the exact date I can't -- I don't think the document has a date on it. As we will see later looking at other documents, in December of 1991, he was a member of the SDS Crisis Staff, and again I'll explain about Crisis Staffs a little later, and was also appointed to the Council of Ministers. On the 27th of March, 1992, when the Bosnian Serb Assembly, which had been established back in October of 1991, passed its Law on Internal Affairs which regulates the police, Mico Stanisic was appointed minister of the interior. He also became a member of the National Security Council, which was established the same day. If we look at one document, number 28, you will see -- we're going to see the document relating to his appointment to the minister of the interior later, but that is the ministerial council, and he appears at number 18. All the names on this list will, I think, become familiar to you as we go through the evidence. It's perhaps worth looking at number 2 on the list: Dr. Vitomir Zepinic, who at that stage was in the BiH police and was assistant minister. Mico Stanisic held the position as minister of the interior until January of 1993. There was then a change of administration and he was replaced, but he was reinstated at the end of that year. Next, Stojan Zupljanin. Again, the photograph you're seeing on the screen at the moment is what he looked like in June of 1992. It's taken from a video which we'll be playing later. He is, in fact, now aged 57, very nearly 58 because he was born on the 22nd of September, 1951. He, too, was a career police officer, in fact, rather more than Mico Stanisic because he remained in the police throughout. He managed to obtain a law degree from Sarajevo University. He joined the Banja Luka police in 1973, and he remained in that area throughout his career. By 1985, he was chief of the Department of General Crime. In May of 1991, he was appointed as chief of the CSB in Banja Luka. Of course, it was still then part of the Bosnian MUP. After the formation of the RS MUP on the 1st of April, 1992, Mico Stanisic appointed him temporarily as the chief of the RS MUP CSB, and that appointment was confirmed on the 15th of May. And if we just look at the date at the top. It's in the middle there, middle of that first paragraph. Zupljanin remained as the chief of the CSB in Banja Luka until February of 1994, when he was appointed advisor to Radovan Karadzic on internal affairs. And we say that in itself shows the close and good relationship he had with Karadzic and the respect in which he was held. So that's a brief biography of both the accused in this case. Can I start with explaining a little bit of the background to the events about which you will hear evidence in detail. We appreciate that it's been said before, but perhaps it's important just to set it in context. As is well-known, the death of Marsal Tito in 1980 gradually led to the decline of the dominance of the Communist Party in the countries which made up the former Yugoslavia, that is to say Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia, Macedonia, Montenegro, and the two autonomous regions, Kosovo and Vojvodina. Those were the countries, republics, that made up the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In November of 1990, the first multi-party elections which were held in Bosnia and Herzegovina resulted in the three nationalist parties, that is to say the Muslim Party of Democratic Action, which was led by Alija Izetbegovic, called the SDA. Obviously it's the initials, the acronyms for the proper titles in the Bosnian language. The Serb Democratic Party led by Radovan Karadzic, the SDS, and the Croatian Democratic Union led by Stefan Kljuc, the HDZ. These three parties received the bulk of the votes. And it's right to say that an assessment of the voting pattern showed that the voters divided on ethnic lines. Following the elections, there was an initial period of co-operation between the three parties in respect of the allocation of posts at both government and municipal levels. And if we have a look for a moment at the diagrammatic representation of that, this shows the power -- the positions in the Presidency and government between January of 1991 and March of 1992. The president obviously being Alija Izetbegovic of the SDA. Underneath that you had as part of the Presidency -- I should say he was the president of the Presidency. Fikret Abdic from the SDA; Biljana Plavsic, SDS; Nikola Koljevic, SDS; and then Stjepan Kljuc from the HDZ; Franjo Boras and Ejup Ganic from the SDA. Prime minister HDZ, deputy prime minister SDA, deputy prime minister SDS, and the second or third deputy prime minister SDA. And then underneath that you will see the minister of the republic secretariat of internal affairs, the RS SUP because it was a secretariat. The Bosnian Serb republic, when it passed its laws we will see and hear changed secretariat to minister, and that's why it became the MUP. And there we see Alija Delimustafic from the SDA. Minister of justice, however, under the SDS. And that gives one a general idea of how the posts were divided after the elections. Gradually, however, tensions arose and mistrust crept in between the three parties. In particular, after Slovenia in December of 1990, and then Croatia in May of 1991, had voted to secede from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and in June of 1991, both republics declared their independence. To try and reverse these actions, the Yugoslav National Army, the JNA, was brought into action for a very brief period in Slovenia and for a longer and more destructive period in Croatia. For various reasons, the members of the JNA who took part in the conflict in Croatia, who responded to the mobilisation call, were largely those of Bosnian Serb ethnicity. According to the 1991 census, members of all three nations were residentially dispersed throughout most of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In rural areas many lived in single-nation villages, but these villages were often adjacent to or close to villages or settlements that were largely occupied by members of other nations. So we should now see on your screen, first of all, simply a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina showing its borders with the other Yugoslav republics. Then if we move to the next map, what you see there are the municipalities that we will be dealing with in the course of this case. Prijedor, Sanski Mostar, Banja Luka, Kljuc, Kotor Varos, Skender Vakuf only because of the Mount Vlasic massacre, that north-west Bosnia going across to Doboj, coming round to Brcko, Zvornik, Vlasenica, Visegrad, the municipalities within the area of Sarajevo, and then down at the bottom Gacko and Bileca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can I just ask you, when you say that Ilijas and Pale were within the area of Sarajevo, are we to understand, just for clarification, do they form part of the Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I suppose you could say they form part of Greater Sarajevo, if there is such a thing. There was central Sarajevo, then there were a number of small municipalities dotted around, one of which was Pale. There are a number of other municipalities within the Sarajevo area. As Sarajevo grew, Your Honours will be hearing a little more about that from Dr. Donia, places which had been completely separate gradually were absorbed, as it were, into the Greater Sarajevo, but Pale is a little bit distance -- the rest of the -- we can probably, and in fact, we will when Dr. Donia gives evidence [indiscernible]. It's right to say that except for a few areas of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was simply impossible to draw boundaries on a map which defined contiguous territory inhabited by only one single national group. They were really very, very mixed. But the Bosnian Serb leadership which was concerned that if Bosnia were to become independent they would be a minority, asserted a claim which was based on their reading of the historical records to 65 per cent of the territory. The fact that much of the territory they laid claim to in this way had a mixed population and contained municipalities which had a majority Muslim population, meant that if pure Serb areas, in inverted commas because again that's an expression that was used, were to be established in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the non-Serb populous would have to be evicted. And one can see in an intercept that took place -- a telephone conversation, sorry, rather than an intercept, which took place between Karadzic and Milosevic on the 24th of October that this was something that was absolutely clear to them. If one looks -- and I'm just going to take parts of this. Now, what Karadzic was saying on the first page, the discussion was going on at that stage as to what was to happen. This was, at the time, when the Bosnian Serbs walked out of the Assembly and set up their own Assembly, the Bosnian Assembly, and Karadzic was saying to Milosevic, talking about Alija Izetbegovic: "They want The Hague, that is Europe, to give them a state in which we would be locked within these borders by international agreements. We can't allow that. We have to prepare everything, and we have to -- and we have prepared everything to create a de facto situation that cannot be ... which they will break their teeth on. They will simply have to break them. There is no way we will live in a country with them. No way at all. That's it." And then later on we go to page 7. At the middle of the page. Let me put this in context. Milosevic says he's going to talk to Izetbegovic, and Karadzic said this: "You tell him the Serbs are moving on, that you can't, that you can't exert influence over us to mellow things down. We are moving on. We will establish full authority over the Serbian territories in BiH and none of his lawyers will be able ... to show his nose there. He will not be able to exercise power. He will not have control over 65 per cent of his territory. That is our goal." And then at the bottom of that page: "Our steps are calculated. We have to establish authority and control over our territories so that he doesn't have -- doesn't get his sovereign Bosnia. Croatia doesn't have control over 30 per cent of its territory, and Bosnia will not have control over 60 per cent of its territory!" During the course of 1991, the SDS established what they called Serb autonomous areas, SAOs for short. Some existed really -- or came to exist in name only. For example, Northern Bosnia. Others, in particular, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, with its seat in Banja Luka, for geographical, political, and military reasons came to wield real power and influence. Its creation, the Autonomous Region of Krajina, was foreshadowed by the establishment in April 1991 of something called the community of municipalities of the Bosnian Krajina, otherwise known by the acronym, which you may see over various documents ZOBK, Z-O-B-K. This community of municipalities set up an Assembly composed of Serb representatives from the municipalities, which were important for the creation of a Serb state, but the reality was that many of these municipalities did not have a majority of Serb inhabitants. That Assembly, in September of 1991, as we will see later, declared itself to be the Assembly of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Intercepts and documents that you will see in this case which were created during 1991 show the increasing determination of the Bosnian Serb leadership to establish that Serb state by force if it could not be done by negotiation. On the 15th of October of 1991, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly declared the sovereignty of the Bosnian republic, and that provoked what is now the infamous speech by Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] And there will be no way to stop that. Now I have to send a message to all the delegates. Gentlemen, believe me, even if you would make such a decision tonight and there is no way to make it because you have a constitutional way whereby we can prevent you from voting, but even if you were to decide that, we would find a way to prevent that in The Hague and to shame Mr. Izetbegovic in The Hague. Also, it would be a very bad image for our peoples, for peoples of Yugoslavia and Europe, and it will be a particular embarrassment for you. It would be to show how disrespectful you are of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I'm asking you one more time, I'm not threatening but, rather, asking to take seriously the interpretation of political will of Serbian people which is represented here by the Serbian Democratic Party and the Serbian Movement of Renewal and some other Serbs. Please take it seriously. Whatever you're doing now is not good. This is the road that you want to take Bosnia and Herzegovina to, that is the same highway of hell and suffering that Slovenia and Croatia took. Don't think that you won't take Bosnia and Herzegovina to hell and the Muslim people to possible extinction. The Muslim people will not be able to defend themselves if we are going to have a war here." He was absolutely right in saying what was to happen was the road to hell. On the 24th of October of 1991, the SDS and the Serbian Renewal Party, known by its acronym of the SPO, their delegates to the Bosnian Assembly, the socialist Republic of Bosnia, they sat as a separate body, and they then proclaimed the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that Assembly called for a plebiscite of the Serbian people in Bosnia to decide whether they wanted to remain within a federal state effectively of Yugoslavia. The plebiscite took place on the 9th and 10th of November of 1991. It was only participated in by Bosnian Serbs. The result was overwhelmingly in favour of staying within the social -- Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and on the 21st of December of 1991, the Bosnian Serb Assembly adopted a decision to establish a republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, and at the same session they appointed the Council of Ministers, which we already had a look at the document of which Mico Stanisic became a member. This council was effectively the precursor of the government which the Bosnian Serbs intended to form in their republic. The republic was formally proclaimed at the Bosnian Serb Assembly session on the 9th of January, 1992. The Serbian -- the republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina was eventually shortened to Republika Srpska in August of 1992. That republic was to come into existence following upon any international recognition of an independent Bosnia. On the 11th of January of 1992, the Badinter Commission, which had been appointed by the -- or established by the economic -- the European Community to assess any procedures by which Yugoslav republics might apply for independence, recommended that there be a referendum in Bosnia to establish the will of its people with respect to independence. And incidentally, on the same day, as we will see, the first meeting of the Council of Ministers was held. That referendum took place between the 29th of February and the 1st of March. The result was overwhelmingly in favour of independence, but very few Serbs voted in that referendum. On the second day of the referendum, a Bosnian Serb guest was killed at a wedding in Sarajevo, and this provided the perfect excuse for the erections of barricades -- for the erection of barricades in Sarajevo by members of or adherents to the SDS. The Muslim members of the SDA responded by setting up their own barricades. Intercept evidence reveals that this was not a spontaneous action but planned and it further reveals, as we will be seeing, the involvement of Mico Stanisic in the barricades incident and support from Banja Luka by Stojan Zupljanin. On the 6th of April, 1992, the European Community announced that it would recognise the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same day, the police academy in Vraca was taken over by the Bosnian Serbs led by Momcilo Mandic, who was then the deputy minister of the interior. So that rather sketchy canter, as it were, through the background, can I now say a little bit about the MUP, the police force. MUP is, in fact, the acronym for the words in Bosnian language of Ministry of Internal Affairs. And I'm not even going to attempt to say it in the Bosnian language. The Law on Internal Affairs, which had been passed in 1990, referred to the republican secretariat of internal affairs. So in those days properly it was called the SUP, but when the Bosnian Serbs promulgated their own Law on Internal Affairs on the 23rd of March of 1992, that referred to the Ministry, and so that's why, as I say, those terms were changed. But in fact, one will see that numbers of people use -- seem to use the terms interchangeably, so you will see SUP and MUP appearing. Either way, whether it's SUP or MUP, it's used to mean the police generally. The structure and the sphere of activities and the powers and duties of the MUP were set out in the Law on Internal Affairs and then further refined in something called the Rulebook on the Internal Organisation of the Ministry or Secretariat. After the 1990 elections in the -- the Socialist Republic of Bosnia MUP, the major posts within there were divided, rather as we saw in the government, by agreement between the three nationalist parties. Now, if we have a look at the chart which was marked 6.3, it was attached to the pre-trial brief, you will see there the Minister Alija Delimustafic; the deputy minister Vitomir Zepinic, whose name we saw in that earlier document, SDS; and then with the, as it were, assistant ministers. The SDA had Avdo Hebib, the assistant minister for police affairs. Again, he's someone you're likely to hear a great deal about. We then go public security, again SDA; the assistant minister for prevention and suppression of crime, Momcilo Mandic, whom you will undoubtedly hear a great deal about during the course of this case; legal and administrative affairs Hilmo Selimovic. Again, he's someone whose name crops up quite a lot. He was SDA. And in fact, we then go -- I don't know we need to trouble about, for the moment, general personnel, administration, analytical information, but the under-secretary for state security service was a gentleman named Branko Kvesic, who was a Croat member of the HDZ. Below that, and I'll come back to that in a moment, we see the CSBs, the centres that existed then, and there were nine of them. We'll have a look later at a map. And then under that the SJBs, which were, as it were, the police stations in the various municipalities, and I'll come back to that in a moment. The regional organisation was based on those nine CSBs, and they were in Bihac, Banja Luka, Doboj -- actually I suppose -- yes, Bihac, Banja Luka, Livno, and coming up you can see where they are all based. That's it. Bihac, right up top, top in the north-west, Banja Luka, Zenica centrally, Livno, Sarajevo, Mostar, Gorazde, Tuzla, and Doboj. That sets out where they all were. The heads or the heads of the CSBs reported directly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, can I just ask you in relation to this chart that you have just shown us. Maybe we can have it back on the screen. And even the one before that with the figures -- with the stations.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The 6.3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: This one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Because it seems to me that although Banja Luka on the map would be geographically the largest area, you have both Tuzla and Sarajevo with more police stations. So my question is: Do the number of police stations reflect the number of inhabitants within that municipality, or how -- what's the relation between the geographical area and the organisation of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Each of the municipalities had its own SJB or police station. As to whether that had anything to do with the numbers of people, you know, I've never actually asked, but I'm sure we can find out. In each of the -- if you look at Banja Luka, you will see that under Banja Luka CSB there was an SJB within the town itself, and then you've got under that Prijedor, Sanski Mostar, et cetera, et cetera. Those were all municipalities, and all came within the geographical area of responsibility, if you like, of Banja Luka. And so the same is for Sarajevo, which had a number of very small municipalities but clearly defined territories, if one puts it that way, or opstinas. Trnovo, for example, was minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The reason I'm asking is that -- that from the indictment one may be led to believe that Banja Luka was the most important CSB of the area, district, and that is somehow counterbalanced by the number of police stations in Tuzla and Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It's Banja Luka after the declaration and establishment of the RS MUP. This is -- what you're looking at here is the pre-break-up diagram.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you see what happens after the break-up, you will see Sarajevo had very few municipalities that were Serb -- I mean, or that could be -- when I say they were Serb, were declared Serb. Banja Luka had a vast number more than appears here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll come this that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The head of the CSB reported to the Minister of the Interior, sometimes through his undersecretaries depending on how busy but it was a direct line of reporting. Each of the CSBs included a state security service, the SSDB. And just to confuse matters, it -- the name for the security service became the SNB at a later stage. This was the intelligence-gathering service. It also contained, the CSB, a public security sector, the SSJB, and the heads of those two services reported to the chief of the CSB. Additionally, however, as you will hear, the head of the SSDB reported to the under-secretary in Sarajevo. At the time when we looked at the chart, that was in fact Branko Kvesic. Those three posts were the major ones within the CSB, but the CSBs contained additionally four other organisational units; a department for communications; a department for foreigners, legal, administrative and personnel affairs all lumped in together; a department for material, financial and technical affairs; and public security stations. And again, the division of posts between the parties applied to the CSB. The CSB had authority over the public security station that we've just looked at, the SJB. The public security -- the public security stations of the municipalities which came within their territorial jurisdiction. And additionally below that, there were local police stations known as SMs, and reserve place stations, SRMs, within the areas of the SJBs. And a person could possibly go mad with the number of acronyms, but you will become familiar with them. If one looks at another chart, one is now looking, and this may be the answer to His Honour Judge Harhoff's question, at the Banja Luka CSB after the split. Are we -- no, we're not. We're looking at the -- no. Yes, we are. Yeah. Absolutely. So we've got Mico Stanisic, and then below that -- just a moment. No, sorry. We're looking at a slightly ... Oh, yes, we are. Sorry. Just a slightly different version. The chief of the CSB going through the under-secretary of public security, Cedo Kljajic, to the minister, but in fact there was also direct reporting. Then under that we see, and perhaps now, Judge Harhoff, we see there are a large number of SJBs which theoretically, in any event, were in charge of their own areas and includes those. They reported to Stojan Zupljanin. And if we move to the left of the chart -- sorry. Right to the left. Thank you. What we see there is the SNB section of the CSB. There was, as I've already said, as it were, a dual system of reporting. The head of the CSB -- the SNB in the CSB Banja Luka, became a man called Nedeljko Kesic. He reported to his superiors in Pale or wherever the MUP happened to be at a moment, who were Slobodan Skipina, and then Dragan Kijac. At the same time, however, he was obliged to report to Stojan Zupljanin, and then below him were the operatives of the SNB. Your Honour, they are slightly different from the chart that we put in -- yes. The reason was we were asked to make certain changes by the Defence. We did, and we obviously didn't give them to Your Honours, which we should have done. Or did we? No, well, we will give them at the end of this because they are slightly different. In fact, as you saw, they slightly took me by surprise because I was still working off the old ones. It's right to say that the authority wielded by the chief of the CSB over the SJBs was a real, not an illusory one nor a theoretical one. To take one example, on the 19th of September of 1991, Stojan Zupljanin wrote to the chief of the Prijedor SJB about the employment of personnel without his approval. As you will see, if we go to the top of the letter first, it's dated the 19th of September, addressed to the Prijedor SJB for the chief, and then begins about he'd been informed that certain people had been assigned to Prijedor SJB. It would appear from the names that all of them were Muslim. And then dealing with Mr. Ilijas Aliskovic, he dealt -- says that was all right, and then he says: "With regard to the other workers for whom I have not provided a recommendation for employment to the MUP of the SR BH and for whom security vetting has not been completed ..." et cetera, et cetera, "I have received reports that they have begun to work at your public security station despite not being covered by the number of police staffing specification posts. I hereby require you to inform me with whom it was agreed that the number of posts in accordance with the Prijedor SJB staffing specification was exceeded and the reason why. I here by require that in all future cases you consult me when proposing candidates ..." The MUP also had a component of reserve police. Just to put it in general terms, and I should say this is a very brief summary of what was actually quite a large and complex organisation, but Your Honours will hear evidence from Dr. Nielsen who will put it in more context. Once a male in the former Yugoslavia had completed his JNA service - there was compulsory military service - he would be assigned to a reserve post. Most often this was with the army, but it could also be with the police. And so basically speaking, all reservists were conscripts, and so the call-up of police reserves was partially governed by the Law on All People's Defence. The only time that the SJBs, the CSBs and indeed the Sarajevo city SUP could call up police reservists without explicit permission or order from the republican MUP was simply for training purposes. Ministerial consent had to be given for the call-up of police reservists, for example, in cases of natural disaster and other exceptional circumstances. Again, all pursuant to the Law on All People's Defence. And indeed, at one stage, I'm not sure that there's a date on this communication, Mr. Delimustafic felt obliged to write to the CSBs about their practices in this respect, and you will see it's addressed to the CSBs, the SJBs, public security service, and indeed to the SUP Secretariat of the Interior. And then it goes on to say under 1: "Public security stations," et cetera, et cetera, et cetera, "can call up members of the reserve police force without the consent of the republic Ministry of the Interior only in order to carry out professional training programmes and training of active and reserve members ..." And it refers to the Law on Internal Affairs. And the reason for that was that in many cases, particularly this was true of Banja Luka, without authority reservists were being called up. The last component of the MUP which is worth mentioning at this stage is that of the Special Police, properly known as the company for the execution of special tasks and duties. This was part of the public security within the SUP, and it functioned as an organisational unit in the seat of the republican -- republican secretariat. It dealt with any complex or emergency operations such as capturing or destroying sabotage-terrorist groups, large-scale disturbances, hijacking, hostages, rescue operations, and all the rest. And it comprised two special tasks platoons and a mechanised platoon. And the 1st Special Operations Platoon undertook the most complex operations that the company faced, while the second one dealt with the rescue operations. And that was all regulated by the Rulebook on Internal Organisation of the Republican Secretariat for Internal Affairs. So there was only that one Special Police force pre the split. So turning now to the events which led directly to the formation of the RS MUP. The Bosnian Serb plans which developed during the course of 1991 to establish a separate Serbian state within Bosnia, as I've already said, of necessity, included a police force as well as an army. The division of the posts and indeed manoeuvering by all three parties within the BiH SUP caused great acrimony. It may well be when you listen to the evidence that it shows that some of the complaints made by the Bosnian Serb leaders about not being allocated the positions to which they were entitled under inter-party agreements or the calibre of people being appointed were not without merit, but the Prosecution say that in this case these grievances, justified or not, did no more than provide the Bosnian Serb leadership with excuses for putting into action that which they intended to do in any event in respect of their police force. Now, it's right to say that Karadzic took a personal interest in the personnel issues which were arising within the BiH MUP, and during the course of 1991, he held numerous telephone conversations on that topic with various people. We're only going to produce one example of a conversation that he had on the 24th of July, 1991, with Vitomir Zepinic, and this was all to do with, first of all, the fact that nothing was to be organised within the -- the BiH MUP without the consent of what he called the Serbs but effectively the SDS. If one goes, first of all, to page 5, Zepinic has been describing a meeting that's been held, and Karadzic says to him: "Please arrange for the collegium to meet every morning and see what happened the previous day and what's planned for that day. So that no one is appointed without the full approval of all the Serbs there." And Zepinic says: "I don't know. I have to consult with Simovic on everything." And Karadzic goes on to say: "Because this will result. We've prepared an alternative which will be atrocious. We've prepared it and we'll fuck their mothers, but to stop that from happening, let them sit every day." And then Zepinic goes on, and then at the bottom of page when Karadzic is dealing with the power, the split of power: "... three peoples are sharing power and watching closely not to be tricked, and we've not been tricked at the MUP, especially at State Security." And then going on to page 9. Again, this is -- the whole discussion is about who's going to be appointed to what. And Karadzic says in the middle of that page: "Again, please let the collegium meet every morning and clear all that out. I was with Izetbegovic last night and with Zulfikarpasic, and I told him right into his face we'll establish a parallel government, parallel police. We'll withdraw our people and they'd have to be paid by the government. We'll withdraw all our people and our arms. We'll establish an entire parallel state if you keep on screwing us." And leaving out the profanity in the middle of that page: "Let there be war, let there be war, but we'll finish the job for once." And then finally over at page 10, Karadzic goes on saying: "Please discuss this matter at the Serbian collegium. And then tomorrow morning at the Serbian collegium you tell them there is this vacant post. Who do we suggest. No one should work on their own." And Zepinic says: "Mico will see me in the morning at 8.30." And Karadzic queries that and he says: "Stanisic, yes." And in fact, Karadzic says, that's not enough either. "Not just Mico Stanisic, we need to assemble everybody." Stojan Zupljanin also took steps to make his dissatisfaction known to the higher authorities. On the 25th of July, he wrote to Biljana Plavsic, then in her capacity of President of the Council for the Protection of Constitutional Order. One can see the date, the 27th of July, to the council -- oh, 1991, to the council of the protection of constitutional order of the SRBH: "Dear, Mrs. Plavsic, I'm writing to you for what might be an unusual and - at first glance - trivial reason, but for me it is exceptionally important for future relations in the Ministry of the Interior." And carries on, he says he was at meeting in the ministry and received a document. And he says: "It wasn't so much the content" -- paragraph 2. "It wasn't so much the content that amazed me as the appearance, or to be more precise, the colour on which it was printed -- in which it was printed. It is a well-known fact that the colour of police equipment is blue, so why then is green suddenly introduced in official correspondence, and is this a sign of the dominance of the Muslims in this important ministry?" And then he refers, as I said, to the two gentlemen that I said the evidence would probably say quite a lot about, Mr. Avdo Hebib and Mr. Hilmija Selimovic: "The attempts -- that attempts are being made to create a Muslim army from this ministry" -- next paragraph. Sorry. "Is also apparent from the most recent police training course that began on the 22nd of July, 1991," and then he goes on about that police training course. Well, he may have described it as trivial, but in fact that letter was taken seriously enough by Mrs. Plavsic for her to read the letter to the council and discuss what should be done about this in no less than three telephone conversations with Radovan Karadzic on the 26th of July, which I'm not going to trouble with at the moment, but they are part of the evidence in this case. Then in the autumn of 1991, two major papers were produced which set out the reasons for and the methods of creating a Serbian MUP within Bosnia. An undated paper ended its proposed course of action with an unambiguous recommendation that a Serbian MUP be established. And if one goes -- the title of the paper was "Possibilities to decentralise internal affairs in Bosnia and Herzegovina." And if one goes to page 3, third paragraph. The paragraph begins with the current security situation in the republic. It says it's "... endangered but still under control thanks to JNA troops that have withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia." Which puts this sometime in early 1992. "The BH MUP with its security services centre and public security stations successfully co-operate with the JNA and in that way it restores trust amongst the Serbian people. The further safety of the Serbian people in BH depends on the successful co-operation between the MUP and JNA, especially in the municipalities where the Serbian people are in a minority." And then the paragraph continues -- perhaps I can finish this document, Your Honour. I'm being reminded that it's probably time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it goes on to say in that same paragraph: "Certain organisational changes and not the decentralisation within the MUP could improve the security and safety of the Serbian people. This could be accomplished by creating a new CSB which would cover the regions of the SAOs ..." Those are the Serb autonomous organisations -- regions. Then the next paragraph, near the end: "The main issue is how to protect the Serbian population in municipalities where they are a minority. Besides that, there is an issue of coordinating the internal affairs, which would provide safety in municipalities where the Serbs are a majority. An expert organ on the republic level should be created in order to carry out these functions. That means that the Serbian MUP must be created." The author of this paper then went on to suggest some solutions to this problem. The first set of solutions presupposed agreement and co-operation with the BiH authorities. The second set did not. "If the previously-stated proposals are not sufficient and the decentralisation should be carried out we propose the following: "1. In the municipalities where the Serbian people are a majority, the SJB should be transformed into municipal police stations. "2. CSBs should be established for the regions of the SAOs which would consist of sectors SDB," as I say, SDB later became SNB, state security service, SNB being national, "and the SJB. They would carry out the compound intelligence duties and coordinate the municipal police stations." And finally, again uncompromisingly: "3. Establish the Serbian MUP at republic level." Then on the 17th of October, so in fact it must have been earlier than this paper, clearly, two days after the BiH Assembly's declaration of the sovereignty of the republic, a paper was produced entitled "The possibilities of organising a Serbian Ministry for Internal Affairs." And I'm not going to trouble you with that because this was obviously the later document. When the Council of Ministers was appointed on the 21st of December, Zepinic was appointed the minister of the interior with Mico Stanisic as the minister without portfolio. The reason for this was that two delegates actually objected to Zepinic's appointment, and one of them, a gentleman named Sarac, actually nominated Mico Stanisic in his place, wherein the end a compromise was reached. Momcilo Krajisnik, who was the president of the Assembly, saying that both of them should be appointed. But it's right to say that dissatisfaction with Zepinic had been expressed by Karadzic since September of 1991 on the basis that he was allowing the Bosnian MUP to become a Muslim force, and we saw something of that in one of the other intercepts. It's right to say that the first meeting of the Council of Ministers on the 11th of January, it was Mico Stanisic and not Zepinic, although he was there, who was given the responsibility of developing the organisation and scope of national security as it was described. So if we look at Exhibit 14 -- sorry, it's my note as 65 ter, but we'll look at the document. Although it's dated the 13th of January, it refers back to the meeting on the 11th of January. And if we go down to the list of attendees you'll see Mico Stanisic, as well as many others. And then if one goes to the third page, item number 4 of the conclusions: "A working group comprising Mico Stanisic, Dr. Vitomir Zepinic, Mr. Lajic, and Mr. Novakovic, will deal with the issues regarding the organisation and scope of national security and will frame a concept about this. Mico Stanisic is responsible for the work of this group." I think that's probably -- Your Honours, I'm about to move to a separate document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Shall we take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think that probably would be sensible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will resume at -- we will resume at 4.05.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, before we invite you to continue, we would alert you that at quarter of 7.00, we would invite you to -- we would invite you to find a convenient point in which you could break your opening so that quarter of 7.00 we may interrupt your opening in order to deal with the matter that you would have raised, and you will pick up -- you will, of course, resume your opening proper tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know that I've raised the matter already, Your Honour, but I was about to mention that we would like some time to discuss the matter which affects the first witness in this case. If that's what Your Honours have in mind, that would be very suitable. So I'm certainly prepared to pause a quarter to 7.00. Your Honours, I think we had reached the -- the first meeting of the Council of Ministers where Mico Stanisic was given the task of developing the -- what's called the organisation and scope of national security. I think I mentioned it already, but just to repeat this, the Council of Ministers was effectively the government in waiting once the republic had been declared. That was the 11th of January of 1992, and then on the 6th of February Radovan Karadzic wrote a long letter which, as we will see, he circulated to a long list of recipients. Just a moment. Yes. Which I hope is coming up on the screen. It is indeed. 6th of February, and it gives the number and if we -- well, we'll go to the next page and maybe it's -- we'll see it's signed by Karadzic. And then it says: "Pursuant" -- at the top of -- "pursuant to the decision of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 2nd of March," which must be a typing error -- or one of them is typing everything [indiscernible], "which relates to the necessary personnel of organisational changes in the Ministry of the Interior, we demand ..." and then it goes in to personnel matters, and under 4 in personnel matters: "4. Personnel of Serbian nationality are to be appointed to posts that belong to them (the chiefs of the public security in Zenica, Livno, and Mostar, commanders in Visegrad)," et cetera, et cetera. Organisational matters, under 2: "The state security sector of the CSB in Sarajevo is to be brought up to strength, the legality of the operation of this sector is to be examined, especially the illegal use of the methods and equipment of this service against officials of Serb nationality (secret surveillance ...)" Now, I'm merely bringing that to your attention because I've already mentioned intercepts -- in this Karadzic was absolutely right. The Serbs were being tapped and much of the evidence that shows the development of the plan comes from this -- these taps. They were, in fact, authorised taps, as you will hear during the course of the evidence. And finally: "I hereby authorise and order Momcilo Mandic, assistant in the MUP of BH, to participate in solving personnel and organisational matters in the MUP of BH on behalf of the SDS." And as you will see, there's a whole long list of people it's delivered to or sent to, and it's signed by Karadzic. I rather feel that it's -- probably is March and the February date is in error but we'll check against the original. Now, on the 11th of February, on the face of it, five days after this letter, perhaps one of the most important meetings that figure in this case was held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, and it was attended -- it was attended by a number of high-ranking Serb police officers, many of whom were to play an important role in the activities of the RS MUP. Notably absent as you will see from this meeting was Zepinic. If one looks at the attendees, Momcilo Mandic you've already heard about, then assistant minister in the BiH -- the Republic of BiH MUP, later to become minister of justice in the RS, Mico Stanisic. Cedo Kljajic. I think you saw his name on one of the charts. Can I -- Your Honours, may I interrupt at this stage to -- to say about the charts. What we propose to do, I know we're no longer indulging in paper exercises, but we will provide proper, new updated colour charts in a folder for Your Honours as soon as the evidence starts. Cedo Kljajic became the under-secretary of public security in the RS MUP ministry. Draskovic became head at some stage of the Trebinje CSB. Stojan Zupljanin. Stanko Stojanovic, for the moment I can't remember. Bjelosevic became head of the CSB in Doboj. This is all under the RS MUP. Nenad Radovic, he became something, and I can't -- ah, yes. He went into the headquarters and was under-secretary in the administration. Tutus became head of the SJB in Banja Luka directly under Zupljanin. Krsto Savic became the head of the CSB in -- and I ought to remember this. It's just been dealt with in Sarajevo. No. Is somebody going to remind me? Krsto Savic. Yeah, Trebinje, I'm helpfully reminded. Goran Radovic, he went into the SNB at headquarters, the republican RS headquarters. Nedjo Vlaski who you will see something about a little later in connection with the barricades incident in Sarajevo in March was also SNB. Malko Koroman, again a name that you're likely to hear quite a lot about, was in the Sarajevo, then Pale SUP. Jesurovic -- Jesuric, sorry, and I ought to know that too, and I've forgotten where he was. Bijeljina. Thank you very much, Mr. Hannis. Then you see there's a gap for the first name, Kesic. That was Nedeljko Kesic who became in charge of the SNB in Banja Luka. And Mr. Velasevic took the minutes. So that's not all of them but a lot of them as you will see became very important. So if we look at the document itself. The first speaker was, in fact, Stojan Zupljanin. Whether it was because outside of Mico Stanisic he was one or more important -- and Momcilo Mandic, he was one of the more important people there or because the meeting was held in Banja Luka he was the first speaker, and you will see that he informed those present: "... that a decision had been made that not a single new Muslim or Croatian employee would be hired until the status of about 600 Serbian police employees from the Republic of Croatia who have fled to Bosnia and Herzegovina has been resolved." The next speaker was Mico Stanisic, and if we go down -- yes. "Work is to be done by the organisation of the Serbian MUP, starting from the municipal and regional levels up to the Serbian ministry. Serbian personnel in the MUP must provide the means to strengthen and supply the Serbian MUP, ensuring that resources will be distributed equally." If we go on to page -- the next page and go to Krsto Savic. You should have it. Krsto Savic has recently been convicted in the War Crimes Chamber of the Bosnia state court. "We are already forming the Serbian Mostar SJB ... "Since Serbs are not being hired at the MUP, I propose that men be taken on without official decisions since there is no other way. I insist that the position of the SJB secretary for the Mostar CSB must not be omitted." And says: "I would mention again that we are already establishing a Serbian SJB on the left side of the Neretva." By February matters were moving on to establish Serbian MUPs as well as Serbian assemblies. Malko Koroman, next page. "My opinion is that all further discussion is pointless. A list of demands should be made drawn up," as opposed to "drown up," "and given to the MUP with a deadline. If they are not met, we must paralyse the whole of SR BH and we can do that." Next speaker was Vlaski who you will hear more about. "We must work out how to carry out the decisions from this meeting. The only way would be to organise the Serbian MUP and implement all the decisions without question." And finally at this end, the conclusions. "A Serbian collegium is hereby established in the SR BH MUP, consisting of Serbian personnel at executive positions in all lines of work." And then item 5: "Not a single decision regarding staffing policies in the SR BH MUP will be implemented without the approval of the deputy minister Momcilo Mandic." The Prosecution suggests - of course, Your Honours, we will be looking at the whole document during -- during the evidence. We've just selected bits at the moment - that this meeting which was not attended by all serving Bosnian Serb members of the MUP. As I say, the notable absentee was Mr. Vitomir Zepinic, was really the beginnings of the, we would suggest, thoroughly illegal in terms of what was happening then, setting up of a separate MUP. It was something that Stanisic and Zupljanin were supporting and organising, indeed, and it was allied with the overall plan that there should be a Serbian state created in Bosnia with, as we'll see, its own police force and its own army regardless of what effect that would have on other nationalities. In fact, after that meeting matters definitely hotted up. On the 13th of February, Mandic sent a dispatch to the leading Serb members of the MUP asking them to arrange meetings with leading personnel in their areas of responsibility. As you will see, addressed to Zupljanin, Bjelosevic, Stojanovic, Savic, and Cvijetic, and then Stanisic. "Following the conclusions ... at the meeting held in Banja Luka on the 11th of February, 1992, please set up and have a meeting with all senior executives of the MUP SRBiH in your area and inform me accordingly." Can I just say one thing? There was, in fact, another Stanisic working in Sarajevo, so one has to be a bit careful as to whether it's addressed to him or to the accused. On the 28th of February, the Bosnian Serb Assembly adopted the Law on Internal Affairs. It came into effect on the 31st of March, and its effect was to establish formally the RS MUP. The new law was based almost entirely on the 1990 Socialist Republic of Bosnia Law on Internal Affairs, and indeed as far as the rulebook was concerned the RS MUP used the old 1991 one throughout most if not all of 1992. A draft after new rulebook was produced in September 1992, but it's not clear that it came into effect then. Article 28 created instead of the old nine CSBs, only five, which were to correspond, as you will see, with the Serb autonomous areas -- districts: Banja Luka, Trebinje, Doboj, Sarajevo, and Bijeljina. On the 24th of March 1992 at the Bosnian Serb Assembly Mico Stanisic was nominated as the minister of the interior, and he accepted that nomination. On the 27th of March, with the promulgation of the Bosnian Serb Constitution, the Bosnia -- the Bosnian Serb MUP was activated. And on the 31st of March, again Momcilo Mandic sent a circular, presumably still in his guise as the assistant minister in the BH MUP, to the personnel of the RS MUP. You see the date at the top, 31st of March, addressed to all the heads of the CSBs, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Then in paragraph 1 he talks about the passing of the constitution, the promulgation of the constitution, and then said in the middle of that paragraph in that -- beginning with the words: "In that respect, pass a law on internal affairs, which will be uniformly applied on the territory of the republic -- the republic of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina as of April 1st and appointed Mico Stanisic until now an advisor in the BiH MUP as minister." The only slight oddity is when he listed the five CSBs which we just looked at under Article 28, there was a change in the last one. Yeah. That instead of Bijeljina, it was Ugljevik. But in fact, in practice, it was Bijeljina. I'm not altogether sure why that is. On April the 1st, Mico Stanisic appointed his CSB chiefs, and on the 4th of April, Vitomir Zepinic sent a letter to the Bosnian Serb Assembly resigning from the MUP. Now, on the 19th of November of 1993, Stojan Zupljanin was interviewed on television. It was some kind of a debate, as you will see, and he gave the reporter then an account of what his goals had been for the RS MUP back in 1992, and we're going to look at the video. Yeah, the -- it's not a dubbed video, Your Honours, so you'll have to listen, and the interpretation will be given.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] I have been dreaming about this new type of police officers, members of the police of the Republika Srpska. As I have put this before myself as one of the goals when I opted, together with several colleagues of mine, to intensively work on preparations that preceded a war, on the one hand, conscience of the risk is existing for the Serb nation and Serb man on this territory. It is my great desire to create a police force that is tailored to the people, although the police is not particularly popular in any system, but we took the English Bobby as our model. We feel they're among top world police officers and that they're highly esteemed and respected by their people, that it is the honour for the English police and the English people when a policeman comes to their houses and that they are above all professionally trained and oriented persons, that they are above all moral and worthy men. When I say moral, it is quite certain that with us in the previous system moral had eroded to its lowest. When it comes to morality, then I have to recall, for example, that we have a similar situation with business morality too. And when I recently found a little time and remembered the nice times when you could read something, I took Aristotle's politics and at one point I found one of his significant thoughts where he said that the most important task of the state is to preserve and foster morality. I think that our state has to do much on this in the forthcoming period. "When it comes to the police it is certain that it must include the most loyal [Realtime transcript read in error "lying"] sons of our people, young, extremely capable and ultimately committed personnel, the persons of reason and clean hands, the persons not interested in personal gain but persons who are willing to give everything, even their lives, for the good of their people." Well, Your Honours, all one can say on behalf the English Bobby is when looks at what actually happened in 1992, that was not, we would suggest, something that was achieved. Can I then move to the actual operational commencement of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I have the intervention in the transcript. I mean, I understand it was very difficult to translate, but there has been quite a few mistakes in the interpretation. I hope this will be dealt with, subsequently, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Can you point us to some of them right away?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Forty-three, it referred to a number of peoples, a peoples, and the most -- it's here lying sons of our people. It's obviously a mistake. I can't remember because I couldn't take the notes, it was very fast, but there is a quite a few mistakes in that. I appreciate that it was impossible for the interpreters to translate from the video, but it can be done subsequently, I guess, reviewed. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm sure ITSS will -- sorry, CLSS will take care of it afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we move now really to the -- to the -- the beginnings of the operation of what we say was the common plan. As I said earlier when I began this opening, the plan of the Bosnian Serb leadership to establish its own state by necessity involved the removal of any non-Serb inhabitants from the planned territory. And when I say "by necessity," of course they could have stayed there but would have had to stay under conditions which would not have been acceptable, and the -- to the Bosnian Serbs it's apparent they saw the non-Serb peoples as a threat. It was abundantly clear, we say, too, that the removal of the non-Serb peoples couldn't happen without the use of force, and that in itself had to involve criminal methods in order to expel the inhabitants. Not only expel them, but make sure they didn't come back. The establishment on the declaration of the Serb autonomous regions were the first public step in the laying out of the territorial boundaries which were intended to form the planned state. And there one sees the adoption of the decision by the community of Bosnian Krajina municipalities on the 16th of September, 1991, which I referred to earlier. And under the agenda: "The adoption of a decision to declare the Autonomous Region of Krajina." And you will see there that the vice-president of the community, Radoslav Brdjanin, a name with which you will become very familiar, was the one who spoke, and said: "By this decision we are ensuring the region's independence. We don't want to bother anyone who does not want to leave Yugoslavia, but no one here can be allowed to put various pressure -- various kinds of pressure on us ... "We are for peace but we do not want that peace to be implemented over our faces as Tudjman and the other leaders want. We know that the Serbs support the army. "By declaring autonomy we want to go to negotiations not to war." As we will see, that is the very opposite of what he was going to say at the 12th of May Assembly of Bosnian Serbs. In fact, the Serb autonomous region of the Autonomous Region of Krajina through Brdjanin wasted very little time in exercising what can only be described, as we've said, parallel authority to the government bodies of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the republic. He sent a telex in October which, as you can see, is addressed to the president of the Municipal Assembly. An order of the SDS. By definition that did not mean the municipal assemblies where the presidents were members of the SDA or the HDZ but anyone who was a Serb or any parallel assemblies that had already been set up. And then he sets out which was by order of the SDS made public at the meeting of all municipal presidents on the 26th of October, 1991, at 3.00 in Banja Luka, chaired by Dr. Karadzic. And then if we go down we can see a list, a long list, of instructions. "Immediately form a command of the town ..." et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Now, all of this was a bit premature, not unusually with Radoslav Brdjanin, and indeed this telex, as you will hear, was intercepted in various places by members of the SDA, and it caused a great furor, and in fact, none of this was ever put into effect. Following the plebiscite in November, the Bosnian Serb Assembly issued a decision making it absolutely clear which territories the Bosnian Serb leadership considered came within the state, and you will see based on the will of the Serbian people in Bosnia as expressed in plebiscite, which of course only Serbs voted, and the conclusion of the Assembly of the Serbian People, the following decision: "On the territories of municipalities, local communes and inhabited places in BH which are considered as territory in the federal state of Yugoslavia." And then if we go to 1, it's quite a complicated sentence but it's wherever the plebiscite was conducted for the Serbian people, where they agreed to stay, and where over 50 per cent of the registered citizens of Serbian ethnicity voted for this common state as well as where the other citizens of other ethnicities voted to remain in the common state "shall be considered to be -- shall be considered the territory of the federal state of Yugoslavia." And then II: "The parts of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina item I of the decision together with the territories of the Republic of Serbia, the Republic of Montenegro, the SAO Krajina, the SAOs Slavonia, Baranja and Western Srem shall constitute the core of the common state of Yugoslavia." And then finally, just to throw in everything, at item III -- sorry. "The municipalities, local communes and inhabited places where the plebiscite was not conducted may opt to remain in the common state from item I of the decision by way of a plebiscite or decision by the Municipal Assembly." So taking everybody in. And then there were further -- if we just look at the end, I think. It's signed by Krajisnik and dated the 21st of November, 1991. Then we come in chronological order -- obviously as I -- can I just repeat, Your Honours, I'm leaving out a lot of the evidence that you're going to be hearing about as to how this developed but just concentrating on the major points. On the 19th of December, 1991, the SDS issued the document which has become known generally as Variant A and B. It has been the subject of argument in numerous trials. It is now an adjudicated fact in this case. Number 100 and 103. Your Honours, that's not surprising, because actual recipients have testified over and over again, and we anticipate you may hear from some in this trial that they were provided with the document and sought to implement it. So again, it is one of the more important documents in the case. This is copy number 93, and we've copied that one for a particular reason which we'll come to at the end. The "Instructions for the organisation and operation of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in emergency conditions." And if we go to the bottom, Sarajevo, the 19th of December, 1991. There's a preamble to all of this which one can see there: "... reasonable grounds for suspicion that certain forces are working persistently, thoroughly and in an organised way to take Bosnia and Herzegovina and thence also the Serbian people out of Yugoslavia by force, we hereby issue these instructions ..." And then going down to paragraph 3. "The tasks, measures and other activities set forth in these instructions shall be implemented over the entire territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or in every municipality where the Serbian people live as follows ..." Of course that's important because in many municipalities they were a minority. In their entirety in those municipalities where the Serbian people constitute a majority, Variant A. And partially in those municipalities where the Serbian people do not constitute a majority, Variant B. "In order to ensure their consistent and timely implementation tasks, measures and other activities shall be set forth in two variants, A and B, and at two levels." Next page, Variant A, the first level and the first two are effectively communication and meetings. Three: "SDS Municipal Boards shall establish immediately Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in the municipality ..." Now, can I just pause there for a moment to give you a very brief explanation in case you haven't come across Crisis Staffs before. It goes back to the old Yugoslavia. They -- when the Municipal Assembly in times of emergency or war couldn't sit, then their duties would be devolved to Crisis Staffs. It's quite a complicated thing. As I say, you'll hear evidence about it from someone who studied this in rather more depth, but the Serbs used this particular type of organisation in order effectively to set up control in the municipalities. It's also right to say that other -- once this had started, once the Serbs started doing it so did the other parties, and so you will hear that there were HDZ Crisis Staffs and also SDA Muslim ones. Anyhow, so immediately establish Crisis Staffs of the Serbian people in the municipality composed of the following: All members of the SDS Municipal Board, persons holding office in the municipality, and, in the middle of that, the chief of the public security station or the police station commander. Effectively it brought together all the people who had authority in a particular municipality. Then what were they supposed to do? "Convene and proclaim an Assembly of the Serbian people in the municipality composed of accept representatives of the Serbian people in the Municipal Assembly. "The first session ... will elect the president of the Assembly which will be president of the current Municipal Assembly or chairman of the municipal" -- except this is all in the municipality where the Serbs were in a majority so the likelihood was the chairman of the -- the president of the Municipal Assembly would be indeed a Serb. Under 5: "Prepare the takeover the staff, buildings and equipment of security services centres and their integration with the newly established organ of the interior at the seat of the centre." Item number 8: "Step up information and propaganda to ensure that the Serbian people are informed fully and in time about the political and security situation in the municipality and beyond." And so on and so forth until we come to the second level. First of all to convene a session of the Municipal Assembly, establish the organs, et cetera, et cetera. Item 2: "Mobilise all Serbian police forces and gradually resubordinate them in coordination with JNA commands and staffs." And then we go on and it's the actual blueprint, as we say, for a takeover. Variant B, very quickly, much the same on the first [indiscernible] until we come to item number 4: "When convening and proclaiming Assembly of the Serbian people, the first session of the Assembly of the Serbian which will elect a president shall be convened by the chairman of the SDS Municipal Board." This of course is where because they were a minority, they were unlikely to have had the president of the Municipal Assembly. Over the page: "Prepare the takeover the staff and some of the equipment of security services centres and their integration with the public security station in the municipality or ... the place where a public security station is established." "In local communes or settlements with a predominant Serbian population establish secret warehouses and depots for storing food and other deficient products, raw materials ... manufacturing ... which should be removed through secret channels from commodities, reserves, warehouses at all levels ..." It never actually mentions arms, but as you will hear, there was a hive of activity in the delivery of arms. Then the second level, I don't think is much the same, although the slight difference is because it was a minority Serb thing. And finally III: "In order to carry out as effectively as possible its tasks, measures and other activities defined herein and also other tasks," et cetera, et cetera, "... judged to be useful for the organisation of the Serbian people for its best possible defence and protection, the Crisis Staff must first undertake a comprehensive assessment of the situation in the municipality and its anticipated development in the next period." "In this, you must ensure and respect declarations of loyalty ... to the constitution and the legal system of the federal state of Yugoslavia by citizens of other ethnic backgrounds." All of this aimed of course at the -- the Yugoslav constitution. And then 3: "Tasks, measures and other activities referred to herein may be implemented exclusively by order of the president of the BH SDS in accordance with a specifically defined secret procedure." And then 4: "The secret procedure for transferring and receiving orders to implement tasks, measures or other activities defined herein shall be established subsequently." I don't think that we've ever recovered the document, if there was one, which established the secret procedures. But as we say, when one looks at the way events developed in the municipalities that form part of this indictment, you will see that they almost entirely, depending on the situation, followed those instructions as far as they were able. Right. And the last page, sorry, this is why we've got this copy, and we -- this is the English translation, and we've also -- it's one of the rare occasions we brought up the B/C/S. Somebody has scrawled on this copy. We don't know who. That's how we got the copy. And you'll see the translation. Can we push it up slightly there -- I'm afraid we can't put it up side by side on -- without using e-court. Thank you. This is Sanction which doesn't allow you to do this, but you will see that 93b is Mico. And can we go back for a moment to the ... yes. And then 93c says "Banja Luka - Stojan." And that's what it says in Cyrillic, apparently. And then down at 93f, apparently, is written something or other Stanisic. Right. Thank you very much. Now, the role of the Crisis Staff as it was envisaged by the Bosnian Serb leadership was set up most clearly in a document which was sent by Djeric on the 26th of April. Well, when I say "sent," there is some discussions whether it was sent or whether it was supposed to have been sent. There were a number of documents which show it try to being recalled, but in any event, this is what he set out. Excerpt from the instructions for the work of the municipal Crisis Staff, and then "in a state of war the Crisis Staff shall assume all prerogatives and functions of the municipal assemblies when they are unable to convene." Paragraph 2 defines who should be members. As I say, those who exercised authority, and you will see in the third line: "Head of the MUP, minister of the interior." Para-3: "The Crisis Staff coordinates the functions of authorities in order to ensure the defence of the territories, the safety of the population and property, the establishment of government," et cetera, et cetera. In fact, we suggest it very odd -- it did the very opposite. In the areas that we're going to look at the Crisis Staff was there to coordinate the various armed forces, amongst others, in order to expel the population, but in a public document that was not what they were going to be saying. 4: "The command of the TO and police forces is under the exclusive authority of a professional staff, and therefore any interference regarding the command of the TO and the use of police forces must be prevented." As you will see, that was -- that was quite an important order, because the Crisis Staffs certainly attempted to give orders at various stages to either the police or the local army units.
