It's quite clear from the evidence that the police and the army stuck to its own hierarchy and took orders as per its own organisation; but nonetheless, it's also equally clear, we would submit from the evidence, that the Crisis Staffs could influence and did influence a number of the actions that were taken, and the stronger the head of the Crisis Staff, the more likely this was to happen. And then finally 7: "The Crisis Staff shall convene a meeting of the Municipal Assembly as soon as circumstances permit to have its work, conclusions and decisions verified." The Crisis Staff actually changed its name over the period. It became at some stage War Staff, War Presidency, but it was always the same body and the same body of men. Most of the Crisis Staffs were abolished in or about July or August of 1992 once the territories had been seized, and then they did indeed give reports to the reconstituted assemblies, but Serb assemblies, not in the territories which had been either Muslim majority or no majority, the mixed assemblies, as it were. Now, in Sarajevo the SDS there held a meeting on the 24th of December to appoint its members of the Crisis Staff, and Mico Stanisic was a member of both this and also, it would appear, the SDS Main Board Crisis Staff, but there we see at number 6 the Crisis Staff is made up of the following members with particular staff, Mico Stanisic. But if one goes to number 2 at the top, yes, there, as I say, one has to be careful where it just appears Stanisic in connection with Sarajevo because there was a Maksim Stanisic, who I believe, but I'm open to correction on this, was some -- was a relative of Mico Stanisic. But as I say, one has to be careful there. And in the middle of that page -- as I say, the argument through every trials is -- about this document has been - how can I put it? - a waste of time, but anyhow, can we look at the middle there. "Particular tasks as per the instructions on the organisation activity of the organs of the Serbian people in BiH in emergency ... according to Variant B under first-degree instructions." Obviously Sarajevo was not a Serb majority -- the city of Sarajevo. The SDS boards in the municipalities which it had been decided should form part of the Bosnian Serb state also wasted little time in putting into effect the instructions. This is the Prijedor Municipal Board of the SDS at a meeting on the 27th of December, and we will see about half -- well, first of all, President of the Prijedor Municipal Board Simo Miskovic made an introductory presentation and then the agenda. If we look at the agenda -- oh, sorry. Can we look at the second -- I'm so sorry. Why don't we switch to the -- yeah. There, above -- the sentence above: "President Miskovic then read out the instructions delivered to the Prijedor Municipal Board of the SDS by the Serbian Assembly." If we go down there: "Establishment of the Assembly of the Serbian People, mobilise the war police." And then Variant II, capital letter B crossed out, first variant. In fact, they were a Variant B. The Serbs were not in a majority in Prijedor. And then: "After the presentation of the instruction Miskovic gave a briefing ..." So that was Prijedor, up in north-west Bosnia. In the Sarajevo municipalities we saw Ilidza proclaiming as a pursuant to the constitution the plebiscite and the instructions number 79, they got apparently, of the 19th of December, 1991, the Assembly of the Serbian People in Ilidza adopted the following decision. And item II: "The Serbian Assembly shall be the highest organ of power of the Serbian people in the area of Ilidza ..." I don't think we need trouble with anything else. Well -- except they sent a copy to - if we go to the next page - to everybody they could think of. The Serbian Assembly, the president of the Main Board, the SDS, et cetera, et cetera, et cetera. Then on the 3rd of March, the incident that I've already referred to, the barricades incident following on the shooting of a Serb guest at a wedding, took place in Sarajevo and I mentioned in passing that it was our case based on the evidence this wasn't a spontaneous arising, erection of barricades, but an SDS planned incident. Can we start with some of the intercept evidence. With -- the first is a conversation between Karadzic and Rajko Djukic -- Djukic, on the 1st of the 3rd, and Djukic was the president of the Executive Board of the SDS. We go down to the middle of the page. He's been describing the beginning of the incident and he said -- and Karadzic says to him: "Get them, get them to rise up and have things prepared. They should close everything tonight." Dukic says: "Erm ... And Radovan Karadzic says: "All the exits. Dukic says: "There is no other way, my friend. Have them close all the exits." And then Stojan Zupljanin, on the following day, got in touch with Mico Stanisic. He gets -- the first thing he does is have a conversation with somebody called Gvozden, explains who he is, and he asks what's going on, and Gvozden says to Stojan Zupljanin: "I didn't know" -- in keeping with that -- [indiscernible] "I think this is how you should also be stepping up the level over there. "Stojan Zupljanin: Yes. Because you can take a turn for the worse." "Zupljanin: Yes, we are also at a level. It just remains to be seen if we will be going for a total blockade or not." Then he asks to speak to Vito, presumably Zepinic. He's told he's not there but Mico is, and he goes on to have a conversation with Mico Stanisic. And Stanisic asks what he's doing, et cetera, et cetera, and [indiscernible] says: "We're listening. "Zupljanin: We are following and listening as they say and waiting for further instructions. Then you are in contact with this policy of yours, aren't you?" And Zupljanin goes on: "For the most part, everything is ready on our side." Mico Stanisic says: "Yes, we are waiting for the sign. If a total blockade is needed or the rest it will be done." As we say, it's clear this was something that wasn't just confined to the SDS, to the MUP in Sarajevo, but was also something that was being, as it were, encouraged by other members of the MUP. In fact, in March nothing happened in Banja Luka or very little, but come April, much the same as we will hear, the same thing happened. At the end of the barricade incident, in which Mico Stanisic was certainly playing a part, a report was prepared by Mr. Kvesic, who was know was the SNB minister, we saw, and it was a report to the government, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and we anticipate you will hear some evidence to suggest that a lot of what was in this report was accurate. Dated the 13th of March, and he says: "We are hereby forwarding you the list of employees ... who took part in the activities relating to the setting of barricades in the region of Sarajevo in early March 1992 ..." First person, Momcilo Mandic, the deputy minister in charge of prevention and suppression of crime. The suggestion is that armed men acting in accordance with his orders. And him distributing jackets and also his presence at the barricade. Number 13 on the list: Malko Koroman, head of the SJB, Novo Sarajevo. Took part directly in the setting of barricades at Lapasnica [phoen]. "His engagement in this action was recorded in radio communication with other participants ..." And then over to the last heard, in the Crisis Staff of the SDS amongst others the following persons were engaged: Mandic; Stanisic; Dragan Kijac, also to play a major role in the RS MUP; Dragan Devedlaka as you saw attended the meeting of the 11th of February; and Cedo Kljajic. And then: "We are stressing that in the critical period ... the inspector of the 1st Administration of BH MUP state security ... Vlaski Nedjo was wounded by fire arms, and he was hospitalised on which the official report was requested from the state security services sector ..." And finally Djevedlaka -- Devedlaka, Radovic, and Blagojevic refused to make any statements about the movements. I mentioned a little while ago that the Variant A and B instructions never really mentioned arms in the storing of warehouses and secret things, but fro late 1991 the evidence, we anticipate, will show that the Bosnian Serbs were arming themselves. Most of those who responded, as I said, to the mobilisation call for the conflict in Croatia had been Bosnian Serbs. The JNA in September of 1990, had taken charge of a large number of the TO, the territorial divisions, the armed forces, from the warehouses in which they had been stored. Yugoslavia had a small standing army but a very large number of people that it could mobilise. And the weapons were kept usually in warehouses in each municipality. Indeed as a 1992 report from Prijedor SJB made clear, weapons were obtained from a number of sources but mainly from the army. As early as October of 1991, Radovan Karadzic was claiming that large numbers of Bosnian Serbs had in fact been armed. And if we look again at another intercept of a conversation this time between a gentleman named Gojko Djogo and Radovan Karadzic and as well early chitchat where he talks to Mrs. Karadzic, and then there's a discussion and of course this is the 12th of October in the Assembly about the Assembly halfway down Alija Izetbegovic spoke two or three times and I had to respond. "Excellent. They say that you told them gentlemen we will not and you can do whatever you want. "We let them but they are preparing for war. They will try to wage war here." Of course this was what Karadzic was publicly saying as well, that it was the -- as it were, the people of who were going for independence of Bosnia that were wanting war and whatever the Serbs did was just to protect themselves. And then down there: "Where is he going to war? "He's crazy. They're totally crazy. What's he thinking to start a war in Sarajevo? Is he crazy? He's, I think, they -- exactly, they should be thrashed if they start a war. They will ... they will disappear." And of course it was a few days later that he made that speech in the Assembly. "There will be rivers of blood." That was certainly a prophecy that came true. Then Karadzic: "They will disappear. That people will disappear from the face of the earth if they start now. Our offer was their only chance. Even that was too much, what we offered them." And then the part that I've referred to at page 7, pretty long conversation, Karadzic says: "They have to know that there are some 20.000 armed Serbs around Sarajevo, that's insane. They will disappear. Sarajevo will be a black cauldron where 300 [sic] Muslims will die. They're not right in the head. I don't know. Now I will have to talk to then openly. People, don't crew around. There are three, four hundred thousand armed Serbs in BiH. What are you thinking of, plus there's the army and the hardware and everything. Do you think you can just secede like Croatia." Probably an exaggeration 3 to 400.000, but, nonetheless, he makes clear the point that they had on their side the army was to be seen and all the hardware that went with the army. And then at another document relating to the arming, this comes from the -- a report in September 1993 from Ilidza, and it talks about what happened, and in terms refers to the army -- the arming. "At the beginning of 1991 during illegal meetings organised by Kovac Tomislav, better known as Tomo Kovac, commander of Ilidza Public Security Station ... policemen of Serbian nationality were informed the war option for realisation of national interests was being increasingly promoted. Aside from the obligations that the Serb gather up and prepare for war through the meetings that took place it was also ... agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality. And the armament was transported from ..." it gives the names of those places. "... 5th of March, 1992, the MUP storage in Dugi Potok was blocked and put under control and the armament and ammunition was distributed to the Serbian people. Blockade of the storage was carried out ... when armament, ammunition, and equipment was supposed to be moved into the city." So the documents produced themselves by the MUP and the Bosnian Serbs show the arming. Now, can we say straightaway it's not our case that clandestine arming was confined to the Bosnian Serbs alone? Both the Muslim and Croats, when they realised the gravity of the situation, tried and succeeded to a limited extent in obtaining arms, but they were markedly less successful than the Bosnian Serbs, both in the quantity and the breadth of weaponry they were able to obtain because they didn't have the access to the army and TO supplies. The importance of the RS MUP in these early stages was made clear by Biljana Plavsic at the Assembly meeting which was held on the 26th of January when she pointed out, it is known what the making of a state means. First, the Ministry of Internal Affairs will do whatever is necessary to have its own army. And indeed Mico Stanisic echoed this sentiment in an interview he gave. It's not altogether clear when it was but it would appear from the context that it's 1994, because it talks about him going and coming back again as minister of the interior. This was an interview on television and again we'll need the earphones, and if Mr. Zecevic thinks there's any fault in what's being said he can translate it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] The history has not recorded of a single example where the police and in this case it is the Ministry of the Interior of a state has become directly engaged in the defence against an enemy's aggression. This is the first time and the members of the Ministry of the Interior have speared headed in the fight against the enemy. It was first the employees of the then Ministry of the Interior in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina who stood up in defence of the Serb national interests. "Stanisic: I would say that this time the Serb people has defended itself from the enemy, given the army that was organised in the way in which it was organised at the time. At the time, the only armed forces among the Serb people were the members of the Ministry of the Interior aware of all that had been prepared against the Serb people and aware of what had in similar situations happened to the Serb people as professional and people who were most at the source of information and normally using our professional knowledge being able to obtain such information in a better manner at the moment while our enemies were preparing to destroy the Serb people in this territory we decided -- or, rather, the members of the Ministry of the Interior decided to prepare the best possible defence of our territory and of our people, defending the people and territory jointly with the people. Reporter: You have this historical role. You have this historical role. You have this historical duty and obligation to complete what you have begun, that is to say, to defend the nation and the Serb land. Tell us, do you have the feeling that sometimes those results are minimised or perhaps even intentionally being kept silent? Stanisic: Well, see, I do not share that feeling simply because I believe that now we all have to work together on this cause of ours, on our common goal, and only in a time to come we will evaluate who made which contribution. I must mention that in the words of Mr. President on the holy -- glory holiday of the Republika Srpska one could clearly see where Mr. President of our republic Radovan Karadzic positions the place and role of the Ministry of Interior of Republika Srpska. Reporter: Of course credit should be given to the ministry and to all of its members for all that has been achieved so far. The special units of the ministry and the police units have been directly engaged at the first front lines of defence against aggression. Tell me, what have been the results achieved in conjunction with units of the Army of the Republika Srpska on the entire territory of our country? Stanisic: Well, luckily for us, both the army and police forces are part of the Serb people with clearly set goals for both of them. Perhaps given our internal tasks, we differ a bit, but when it comes to the defence of our country and defence of our people, then we are all one, one united front. The armed forces include both the army and the police and even all the Serb people in this territory."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In particular, of course, it's the passage where he stated that at the time the only armed forces amongst the Serb people were the members of the Ministry of the Interior. On the 18th of March at the Assembly, Krajisnik referred specifically to the need for ethnic separation on the ground. A delegate called Vjestica from Bosanska Krupa made it clear that a Serbian MUP was necessary so that they could seize control physically of their territories. And one of the methods of seizing control was the use of the so-called paramilitary forces. On the 3rd of April, so almost exactly a month after the barricades in Sarajevo, a group styling themselves the SOS invaded, in inverted commas, Banja Luka and set up barricades. And in what was almost a repetition of the Sarajevo barricades indent, the SOS issued a set of demands that effectively were designed to establish Serb control in Banja Luka. It was the job, of course, of the MUP in Banja Luka, headed by Stojan Zupljanin, to remove the barricades and restore order. Not surprisingly, no such thing happened, and we anticipate the evidence will show is that is because this was something that Stojan Zupljanin knew about in advance. It was deliberately planned by the Bosnian Serb leadership in conjunction with the MUP in order to, as it were, advance the cause of the Serbian people. It's also right to mention at this stage, as you will hear, that a group calling itself the SOS also took part in the events which led to the takeover of Sanski Most, and it's worth having a look briefly at the report that appeared in Glas newspaper about all these events. It's a very long report. I'm just going to highlight some of it. This -- what you've got here -- you're going to see is, in fact, the newspaper. It's got sort of boxes all over the place, but this is just how it's been set out in the translation. Banja Luka, 3rd of April. Since this morning the city of Banja Luka has been blocked. The members of the Serbian defence forces, SOS, have seized all key intersections in the city and control the Municipal Assembly ... Radio Banja Luka, et cetera, et cetera, all the bridges and important strategic positions in the city. They were, as you will hear, a very small group of men, and as I say, there's no earthly reason, particularly when one looks at the raid that we're going to see -- that happened in May, the equipment that was available to the Banja Luka CSB and SJB. Then what did they proclaim, the Serbian defence forces? "We, Serbian patriots, patriots, members of the JNA, reservists, volunteers, citizens of Banja Luka, relatives and friends of fallen soldiers, organised in the Serbian [indiscernible] ... have decided on the step because of a new genocide against the Serbian people and the failure of all mechanisms for the protection of the Serbian people." It says in the explanation of this morning's appearance of barricades on all the approaches to Banja Luka. "The whole announcement concerning the barricades was read out over Radio Banja Luka, but with no explanation about which political forces - parties - are actually behind the SOS." And then it goes on further down of the page, yep: "Therefore," the statement says, "we demand that the president of the municipality activates a Crisis Staff that we would agree to and negotiate with so as to fulfil the following demands." Amazing enough those demands seem to fit in with the Variant A and B instructions and the general goals of the Serbian people. "We demand the president activates a Crisis Staff, that there's an immediate enactment on a Law of Internal Affairs of the republic of the Serbian people, territory of Banja Luka, Bosnian Krajina. Dismissal of all employees who have shown in their work they are destroyers of Yugoslavia and enemies of the Serbian people," and that of course meant non-Serbs. "No disbanding of the Banja Luka Corps. Arrest of war profiteers and the like, investigation." And then the next page. Yep. And then: "Large-scale abuses, we demand extraordinary sessions of the Municipal Assembly and the Krajina Assembly can be convened so the Crisis Staff can appoint its officials." And then, SOS, I think -- yeah. And then almost immediately -- surprising enough this was a genuine incident where effectively a gun was being placed at the heads of the police, Municipal Assembly, the same day the demands are all accepted. Predrag Radic, president of the Banja Luka Crisis Staff -- and can I interpose at this stage just to explain. You will hear that there were, in fact, two Crisis Staffs based in Banja Luka; one was the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, one was the one which was based on the Municipal Assembly in Banja Luka, and the Crisis Staffs as discussed in the Variant A and B instructions. Predrag Radic, who was actually president of the Municipal Assembly at the time Banja Luka was a Variant A municipality, declared that all the Serbian defence force demands had been agreed to. True in a slightly modified form. And then it talks about the negotiations, and then during -- yeah. "At a press conference in which Predrag Radic, Dr. Radoslav Vukic," he was president of the SDS board and you'll be able to see what he looks like at the 12th of May Assembly, "Stojan Zupljanin, Radoslav Brdjanin, and Mr. Milinkovic replied to numerous questions by reporters ..." And then if we go on, Stojan Zupljanin used this opportunity to emphasise the situation was extremely difficult in other areas, particularly in the peripheral areas of the Bosnian Krajina on the Kupres plateau. Closing the press conference, et cetera. And then we see the people who were to be on the Crisis Staff. Radic, Zupljanin, Tutus. Milorad Sajic, he was in charge of the TO. Kesic, Vesic. Puvacic, to my recollection, was the air force. Colonel Bosko Kelecevic was the intelligence arm of the still then-JNA, and Subotic from the Banja Luka corps. Dr. Radoslav Vukic and Nenad Stevandic. Nenad Stevandic, again, was to play a major part in these events. At that stage he was president of an organisation calling itself Sokol, which was -- it actually, I believe, means "hawk," but it was supposed to be the young, politically engaged Bosnian Serb organisation. He then went on to become quite a powerful figure and a member of the so-called Banja Luka Special Police. Right. And that's the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, is this a convenient point at which to take the break?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours. Your Honours, after that incursion by the SOS -- after that incursion into Banja Luka by the SOS, the situation was rather succinctly summed up in a report by someone or a group calling themselves Milos. You will see a number of documents in this case from this group. They were a group of Serb -- Bosnian Serb police officers working under the Banja Luka SNB gathering intelligence. And on the 15th of April, they sent in a report to the Banja Luka CSB, first of all dealing with an apparently attempted assassination of Nenad Stevandic. As I said, he's going to figure quite often in this case. But then they went on to say this: "We ask you for an urgent contact with the centre in the purpose of clarifying, explaining, the certain circumstances which are neither in your nor in our favour if we want to succeed in executing the forthcoming tasks." And it goes on then: "The self-named Serbian dukes, leaders and ring leaders hold the majority of the SDS leadership in their surrounding and under their control, and they have the strong armed groups by which they threaten anybody who do not think the same way they do and who do not act the way they would like." And we would suggest that that was a fairly accurate summary of what was going on from, in fact, a group of Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Madam Korner, was the Milos group self-appointed or --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. It was an appointed intelligence-gathering organisation which acted under the code-name Milos. It contained a number of people in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So it was not just a private --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: -- gathering or getting together of intelligence police officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. No. They were an authorised intelligence-gatherers, but some were perhaps more sensible and realistic than others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And may I say, it's an unusual -- unusually frank and perhaps one might say honest report. In other reports one will see the use of the standard anti-non-Serb terminology. On the 6th of April, with the recognition of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina, the very first action by the RS MUP, as I've mentioned already, was the forcible takeover of the police school in Vraca. That then became the first headquarters of the RS MUP. The headquarters in the period 1992 moved around quite a lot. It was in Vraca, in Bijeljina, in Pale. The attack on the school was executed under the leadership of Momcilo Mandic and a man named Milenko Karisik. Karisik had been the second in command to the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina Special Police. The takeover, in fact, perhaps not surprisingly, involved taking hostages, and it would appear that before they were released, exchanged, there was subsequent ill-treatment. Now, Mico Stanisic, it would seem, had a close relationship with Milenko Karisik and the Special Police generally. In June of 1992, a Serb -- Serb filmmaker but based, I think, in England at the time, made a very long documentary, which was eventually shown on British television, called "Serbian Epics," or Epic. And we're only going to show a part of it now, but during the course of the filming they had a brief conversation with Stanisic who was apparently engaged in the training of the Special Police troops, and it is actually, I think, in English. All right. I'm -- anyhow, it is subtitled, Your Honours, so you won't need the ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Karishko Miljenko, commander of the special unit of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina MUP who commanded the first operation. His assistants Brdar, Zlatko, commander of the unit in that first operation and he commanded his unit. Mane, also an associate of Mr. Karishko who took part in this first combat and commanded his unit. Skoro Spaso also an associate of Mr. Karisik who participated in the same operation and commanded his unit. And Mr. Abazovic, Goran, who has been with me from the very first day."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As I say, that's a small portion of what is, I think, well over an hour's film. On the 15th of April, a joint session of the National Security Council and the government decided, amongst other things, to ask the Presidency to declare an imminent threat of war. You will see there the people who attended the meeting, and then if you go down to item 3, we can do this fairly quickly, decisions and conclusions. "Reviewing the security situation the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was assessed ... the conditions are being met to propose that the Presidency of the republic declare an imminent threat of war." Now, during the course of April 1992, the forcible seizure of power by the Bosnian Serb leaders, municipal leaders aided and abetted by the higher leaders, took place in the majority of the municipalities which are the subject of this indictment, and in nearly all, the events began with the takeover of the SJB. If we look for a moment as an instant guide to the chronology that was attached to the pre-trial brief, you will see there between the 12th -- sorry, the 9th of April, Zvornik came under the control of the Serb forces. 12th to the 14th, Visegrad. 14th to 17th, Vogosca. 19th of April -- sorry, 17th of April, Bosanski Samac. Sanski Most on the 19th. 20th, 21st, Vlasenica. 30th, Brcko, Prijedor, Doboj. Now we are -- actually, we're now heading into May, so we'll leave that. And if we can show this graphically depicted. All right. The -- what we're showing you at this stage, and we may as well show the whole thing, is the municipalities that were taken under Serb control. The red -- those in red are the ones which figure in our indictment, but it's obviously important that it is realised that that is only really quite a small proportion of the municipalities that were taken over by control. And what we saw is, as you can see what is underneath -- if we can right it back again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, the turning red occurred over how long time?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right until the end of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: From April to July --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. It took, though, very few, most, as you can see, if you looked at the list, April and May is when most. Some it took a lot -- it took a little longer. For example, Kotor Varos which I'm going to concentrate on as an example. But we'll see there -- yeah. I think we saw Kotor Varos as one of the last.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't see [Microphone not activated] --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's -- the two at the bottom are Bileca and Gacko. And above -- just so you understand, above the municipalities at the top of the picture into Croatia was the Knin part of Croatia, which there was also fighting going on and what's called the -- the Serb Republic of Krajina. And towards the east we're talking about Serbia. Right. As far as the RS MUP was concerned, once the takeovers were effected, all officers were required to sign a loyalty oath to the Serbian republic. On the 16th of April, Mico Stanisic ordered all CSBs to forward a list of non-Serb employees that were within their area of responsibility, and the same day, Stojan Zupljanin sent an instruction in respect of the loyalty oath. As we will see, the penalty for failure to sign was extended leave, in reality dismissal. In some places we'll see, for example in Bileca, the Muslim employees weren't even given the opportunity to take the oath. So the first document that we're looking at is the order dated the 16th of April, by Mico Stanisic, number 01?4 above the date of the 16th of April. Incidentally, what it says in the first paragraph is: "Every day forward a daily report to the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BiH," and gives a fax number. And then: "I therefore order that by no later than 2400 hours on the 16th of April ... all centres and SJB stations in the territory ... forward aggregate reports on the number of Serbian and non-Serbian employees who have been employed at the Ministry of the Interior." And then: "Because of problems with communications, the above-mentioned centres must inform all SJBs in their territory of the contents of this dispatch." And then on the same day Stojan Zupljanin received -- sorry, a response from Prijedor, that station, referring to the solemn oath which he'd been asked to -- and says -- which says this: "The obligations mention this had telegram, i.e., to sign the declaration do not apply to the Prijedor and Kotor Varos SJB. Authorised officials at the stations may continue to wear the current insignia if they wish until further notice." That was because the Serbs had no overall majority in either of those two places. And finally, dealing with the Bileca document. At the beginning page you'll see this is from the CSB at Nevesinje in Sarajevo. Don't worry about the first, but then it's a list of people who received a salary, those who were on active duty, and finally: "Employees of Muslim nationality from the SJB Bileca and SJB Kalinovik were not offered the possibility to express loyalty to the Ministry of Internal Affairs of the BiH Republika Srpska, so we are not able to inform you if they did express loyalty." By May of 1992, the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff had publicly announced its existence and started to issue decisions. One of the most important related to the deadline for surrender of weapons, and in practice, although as we'll see the order doesn't say specifically that, this order for disarmament was only executed as against the non-Serbs, the Muslims and Croats. The first document is that of the 18th of May, which is the conclusions of the Crisis Staff meeting. First of all, it says: "A delegation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina consisting of ... Kupresanin, ... Erceg ... Sajic and Stojan Zupljanin is to go to Pale and hold talks on defining the territory towards Semberija." This came after the Assembly meeting of the 12th of May, which we'll look at in a bit, but I wanted to deal with the disarmament things. And then item number 4: "All formations that are not in the army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the Banja Luka Security Services Centre and are in the Autonomous Region of Krajina are considered paramilitary formations and must be disarmed." As I say, it doesn't say that in terms, but clearly the Muslims and Croats would not be joining the RS MUP or the army of the Serbian republic. "All those who are not part of the armed forces of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or its police must return their weapons." And then item 6: "The Banja Luka Security Services Centre is to write instructions for the disarming of paramilitary formations." And then over at paragraph 15: "A meeting is to be held in Mrkonjic Grad with a delegation from Jajce. The delegation of the Autonomous Region of Krajina shall consist again of ... Kupresanin ..." Kupresanin was at the time or had been the president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Assembly. However, Radoslav Brdjanin, as we will see, became president of the Crisis Staff. Radic, who was the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. Sajic was the TO, and Stojan Zupljanin. The Crisis Staff itself, as I say, declared itself on the 5th of May, and there we see number 1: President Radoslav Brdjanin, and then General Talic. As we saw, the instructions were to gather together everybody from -- who was of any importance. General Talic was then the head of the Banja Luka Corps, the 1st Krajina Corps of the JNA. It hadn't yet transformed itself. And if we note also number 14, Slobodan Dubocanin, who was about to obtain infamy in Kotor Varos. Zupljanin is number 10, and Nedeljko Kesic, head of the SNB in Banja Luka, also a member. 9th of May. This is actually leading up to the document we just looked at. This was the -- at this stage they're calling themselves War Staff. As one sees, there was War Presidency, War Staff, Crisis Staff but it's all the same lot. And there we see: "The weapons should be turned over to the nearest public security station by 15 hours on the 11th of May ... at the latest." And the next bit: "Firm action will be taken against those who refuse to return weapons." We shall see what the firm action was. In some cases whether or not weapons had been handed over, firm action was taken. And then on the 11th of May, back to calling itself a Crisis Staff. Deadline extended to the 14th of May, 1992. "After the expiry of the deadline, the weapons will be seized by the employees of the security services centre of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the most severe sanctions shall be taken against those that disobey the proclamation of the Crisis Staff." On the 20th of May, Stojan Zupljanin sent out a dispatch about the conclusions which had been reached at the meeting of the Centre council of the security services, and you can see there who attended. In addition to members of the council of experts, the chiefs of the SSJB and the heads of departments in the CSB, this was a council within the MUP: "The meeting was attended by the chiefs of the public security stations in Banja Luka, Gradiska, Dubica, Grahovo, so on and so forth. As I said, once the split came Banja Luka became the largest of the centres for the numbers of SJBs and territories within its area of responsibility. Then, first of all, Stojan Zupljanin presented an overview of the current security station, and what he then -- in summing up, he proposed the following to be adopted as conclusions, and the most important was number 4: "All my orders conveyed orally, as well as those I may forward by dispatch, must be carried out: They are your law. The chain of command, commanding an execution are clearly distinguished in this service. If any one of your staff should refuse to act upon an order, just inform him he's fired; we have got to get ride of the old ideology and concepts not suited to the present moment." We suggest that one small sentence, paragraph, really sums up the personality and the control that was exercised by Stojan Zupljanin. If we go over to -- for a moment to some of the conclusions, because these also go to other themes that go to the case. Item 12: "Chiefs of departments in the CSB headquarters and chiefs of public security stations will submit monthly performance reports and plans for the current month to me by the 5th of every month. I will deduct 10 per cent of the chief's income for every failure to submit a report on time." One of the major aspects of the RS MUP and other MUPs within the former Yugoslavia were that they were disciplined, hierarchical organisations, and although the beginnings of the period that we're going to be looking at from April until the end of May, obviously things were a bit chaotic from everything that was going on, nonetheless, the obligation to report was enforced. Stanisic was insisting the CSBs reported to him. The CSBs were insisting that the SJBs. And although again one will see obviously that communication was occasionally a bit erratic, they had many methods of communicating, and indeed did continue to communicate throughout the period. And then paragraph 14: "The chief of CSB will arrange with the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina to make a decision in accordance with Article 510 ... which will entitle the Banja Luka Security Services Centre to acquire all confiscated ownerless property ... to sell it and to use the profits for the equipping of the service. This primarily concerns seized motor vehicles of unknown origin or vehicles acquired in a criminal way: They are to be handed over to the centre where they will be registered as service vehicles." One of the -- again one of the themes running through this is that there appears to have been whole scale, in some areas, appropriation of motor cars by members of the MUP. There is a particular factory where a number of Volkswagen Golfs disappeared from that -- appears to cause some consternation. Right. Now, the -- as I say, those orders for disarmament provided the excuse for the attacks on the non-Serb villages and areas. On the 12th of May, the Bosnian Serb Assembly met in Banja Luka. It was, again, an extremely significant meeting. It was the one in which the strategic goals of the Bosnian Serb leadership were enunciated clearly for the first time, and what that implied was set out by one of the deputies, a man called Kalinic, and subsequently approved by Radoslav Brdjanin in a speech. And at the same time, the Assembly took the decision to establish the -- its own Bosnian Serb army which is known generally as the VRS. I think that's Vojska Republika Srpska. So the Assembly not only set out the goals that were to be achieved but established the second mechanism by which it was to be -- or they were to be achieved, the VRS, which together with the MUP were to be the direct architects of some of the major crimes. If one looks, first of all, at a couple of things in the actual record of the Assembly, and then there's a video, a short one, showing who was attending. Can we just go to the first page for a moment. Sorry. This is the minutes of the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina, 12th of May, Banja Luka, chaired by the president of the Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik. The first speech was that of Krajisnik, and then Dr. Karadzic, Radovan Karadzic, made a very long speech, though not as long by any means as that made at the end by Mladic, and this is part of that speech that he made. This is page 13. "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency, the government, the Council for National Security which we have set up, have formulated strategic priorities, that is to say ... strategic goals for the Serbian people. The first such goal is separation from the two national -- the other two national communities - separation of states. "Separation from those who are our enemies and who have used every opportunity, especially in this century, to attack us, and who would continue with such practices if we were to continue to stay together in the same state." As I have no doubt you're aware, there is continual harping back in speeches to what happened in the Second World War, in particular. And again, it is suggested that all the actions of the Bosnian Serb leadership are simply to defend themselves. The second strategic goal is the corridor between Semberija and Krajina of the utmost strategic importance for the Serbian people because it integrates the Serbian lands not only of Serbian, Bosnia, and Herzegovina -- because it integrates the Serbian lands not only of Serbian, Bosnia, and Herzegovina, but Serbian, Bosnia, and Herzegovina with Serbian Krajina, Serbian Krajina with Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was to form particularly in north-west Bosnia, where Stojan Zupljanin was operating, one the most important reasons for the actions that were carried out, as we saw from that chart when the municipalities lit up, there was -- the determination was to link up with the other Serbs. Third strategic goal: The corridor on the Drina valley. Fourth strategic goal: Establishment of the border on the Una and Neretva Rivers. Fifth strategic goal: The division of the city of Sarajevo into Serbian and Muslim parts and implementation of an effective state government in each of these two parts. And that, of course, leaving aside the military considerations for establishing a corridor was also going to be a major task because Sarajevo was ethnically diverse even though some particular areas might have of more of one nation than another. And the sixth strategic goal: Access of Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the sea. This was all said in the Assembly at which a large number of people were present, including reporters -- in fact it wasn't actually officially published in a gazette until considerably later, I believe the following year. Now, it is worth looking at a speech by Dragan Kalinic who, I believe, became the minister of health, and what he said was this: "I'd like to address some of the things I've heard here and some of the information and ideas have been in circulation recently and this would be the right place to clear such issues up while there is still time. Among all the issues this Assembly should decide on, the most important one is this: Have we chosen the option of war or the option of negotiation? I say this with a reason and I must instantly add that knowing who our enemies are, how perfidious they are, how they cannot be trusted until they are physically, militarily destroyed and crushed," which of course implies eliminating and liquidating their key people. "I do not hesitate in selecting the first option, the option of war ..." "Why do I say that the option of war seems more likely to me? Because only what has been conquered militarily may become really and truly ours." And when Radoslav Brdjanin, who we saw earlier in a document saying everything should be peaceful, rose to his feet - page 29 - he said: "... I asked for the floor only after I realised that I was the most remote, that compared to everyone else I am the kindergarten. I would first of all like to thank all those participating in the discussion, and I would like to say a heartfelt bravo to Mr. Kalinic. In all my appearances in this joint Assembly, it has never crossed my mind is that although he seems quiet, while I seem hawkish, his opinions are the closest to mine." And Radoslav Brdjanin, in his position as president of the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff was in a position to put that, his views of what should happen, namely war, into effect. And over the page, still Brdjanin speaking. What he said there relates to the issue. "How can anyone still believe," he says, "it is all right that we have a Muslim teaching political classes in the Banja Luka Corps?" Shortly after this, which created the VRS in June of 1992, all Muslim and Croat officers were dismissed from the VRS, and this was a reference to a professional soldier called Colonel Osman Selak, and it showed that Brdjanin was not averse to even putting pressure on the military to get rid of its non-Serbs. And finally the president, Hadzic, who was present here and who I think we see in the video, is the one who was president of the Croatian sub-Krajina so-called, and the missing -- one of the last missing indictees in this institution, as everyone knows, and there: "As for military options, I do not know much about that, but I propose, as Mr. Zupljanin has said, that Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina cannot be defended if it is based on the voluntary principle. If we establish Serbian armed forces today, we will be announcing general mobilisation and now everyone must be put under the command of the Serbian armed forces and the forces for preserving law and order. All paramilitary units must truly disappear ..." As we will see later, that was more an expression, I think, of pious hope. And I think we'll have to look at the video tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner. I would now invite Judge Harhoff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- administrative issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The issue that we wanted to raise was the manner in which and the basis on which Dr. Donia is to be examined when he arrives here, I believe Wednesday, because it was -- it became clear to us that the issue which we had discussed earlier on relating to the late filing of some documents pertaining to Dr. Donia's testimony, expected testimony, was such that one of these -- some of these documents related to a report that Dr. Donia had filed regarding the siege of Sarajevo, and that report, that last report filed by Dr. Donia, was then dubbed the Karadzic report. And since it had been filed late, the agreement was made that the Defence counsels would then be entitled to have a two-month period in which to study the importance of this late document. Now, we also took the liberty of going through the document, and it became -- a question arose to the Bench, namely of the relevance of this report and of the 29 documents that have been identified in the late filings as being relevant to the Karadzic report, because the Chamber is mindful that the siege of Sarajevo as such falls outside the scope of this indictment, and therefore, at least by a first glance, would seem to be irrelevant to the case and something that we really shouldn't concern ourselves with unless you can point us to the parts of the Karadzic report and the documents that pertain to this report and also to the 29 documents that you have identified that are relevant to this report, unless you, in all of this material, can point us to the issues that are really relevant to this trial. So the two questions we have is which -- first of all, which parts of the Karadzic report do you hold are relevant to this trial, and we're asking this because you have in your motion yourself use the expression that some parts are relevant to the present case. Now, we want to know which parts are you thinking about, or which parts are you talking about. And secondly, which of the 28 documents that go along with the Karadzic report relate to the Karadzic reports itself? We would like you, Mrs. Korner, to come back to us when you have completed your opening statements tomorrow and to show us which parts are relevant in the report and which of the documents are relevant, and we will then strive to rule on the matter immediately, because we think that the Prosecution should be told right away, before Dr. Donia appears as a witness, whether or not he should be examined and cross-examined at all on the basis of the Karadzic report and the documents that go with it. Now, the difficulty is that if after having heard your submission tomorrow, if the Chamber reaches the conclusion that we really don't think that it is appropriate in this trial to engage in a major examination and subsequent cross-examination of Dr. Donia on matters relating to his Karadzic report, then there will be no need to call him back at all after two months, because then that whole issue falls away, which in turn implies that once the Prosecution has exhausted its three hours of examination-in-chief of Dr. Donia, then the Defence would be required to proceed immediately to the cross-examination, because if I have understood you correctly, you have indicated that you are ready, both teams, to enter directly into the cross-examination of Dr. Donia upon his report, except for the Karadzic report. But if the Karadzic report falls away, then you should be able to proceed straight away to the cross-examination of Dr. Donia. And that implies in turn that if Dr. Donia expects to be able to return to the US on Thursday, that might simply not be possible. I don't know how you're going to handle this, but I would add that -- that when witnesses are being called for examination and possibly for some cross-examination, which had been advised by the Defence teams, witnesses should be ready to be available for the entire exercise. But let's just -- I'm just putting these things to you, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think we better --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but it really is quite important. Dr. Donia, I think, is about to get on a plane right now. He cannot, under any circumstances -- he's a professional man, Your Honour, and he has commitments, and the trial here has been undergoing a number of changes in when we were sitting, when it was starting and the like. So he cannot be here on Friday. The difficulty also that we now face is that clearly, and we were -- we have gone through with Dr. Donia what we considered to be the relevant -- what we considered to be the relevant documents which could be dealt with in a three-hour examination-in-chief. We served his report -- sorry, we filed his expert report on the 14th of August, and we haven't heard any -- any suggestion that it wasn't relevant, and I can and will deal with this in full tomorrow. But if this is the situation, rather than putting the Tribunal to the not-inconsiderable expense of having Dr. Donia here, who will have to leave on Thursday, and not at the moment knowing what evidence I will be permitted to lead from him, or he knowing that, or indeed whether or not cross-examination is going on, would seem to me to be an undesirable situation. And the reality is he's a private citizen, Your Honour, who's given up considerable time to preparing reports and testifying here, but he has this unbreakable professional commitment on Friday in the United States.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: It's a gamble, it seems to me, on the part of your team to expect we would be able to finish him off on Thursday. So I think -- I realise the difficulty, but I also must say that -- that it seems to me to be a little imprudent, actually, to expect that you would be able to conclude your examination-in-chief and the two Defence teams would be able to put all the questions that they might have in cross-examination on anything apart from the Karadzic part in one day only.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, Your Honour, it would assist, because we've had various counsel-to-counsel discussions on the matter perhaps if you were to inquire of Mr. Zecevic and Mr. Pantelic how long they think, leaving aside the Sarajevo report, they would wish to cross-examine. Our understanding has been up till now that they would be able to complete such cross-examination as they wanted to on earlier other matters that he deals with certainly by Thursday at 12.00. If that's not the case or they are not able to give the Court such an assurance, well, then, Your Honours, the only thing we can do is to stop Dr. Donia coming at this stage, particularly as you now raise the question of whether it's relevant or not and wish to hear argument on that. And we'd have to do that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That clarifies the situation a bit, in my view, because this means that if you take the maximum of three hours and Mr. Zecevic has announced that he will use a maximum of one hour, and if you assume that Mr. Pantelic will not put any cross-examination because Sarajevo is not relevant to his client, then we might be able to actually complete the whole thing in one day.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that -- Your Honour, well, that's certainly the basis on which we've been working, and obviously knowing that administratively it was important, we have engaged in the hopes of helping the Court, as I say, in inter-counsel discussion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'll just consult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Maybe I could just clarify. What is actually the time that you have asked for in consultations with the Prosecution for the cross-examination of Dr. Donia on anything except the Karadzic report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, last week we were -- we received a mail from the -- from the legal officers inquiring about the time of our cross-examination, and we estimated the time between three and four hours for the part of the examination concerning the original Dr. Donia report. I'm not sure where my learned colleague found the one-hour figure. We never discussed that. I don't think so at least.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I didn't say an hour. I don't think so, at least.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on. And, Mr. Pantelic, do you intend to cross-examine Dr. Donia?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we informed the Senior Legal Officer that our intention is to cross-examine Dr. Donia for one hour and a half. That is our position. Although just for the record, Your Honour, I think that his report is absolutely irrelevant [Realtime transcript read in error "relevant"] for this case. It's background. It's history. This is a criminal case, Your Honour, but we shall make further submission on that issue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Back to you, Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly -- I did -- I never mentioned the figure one hour. My understanding was that Mr. Zecevic, from the communication we -- I think Mr. Pantelic wants to say something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Just for intervention for the transcript I said that Dr. Donia report, it is page 85, line 6, line 6. I said Dr. Donia report is totally irrelevant for this case because this is a criminal case and we have to deal with the criminal subjects and categories and not with the poems, history, speeches, et cetera. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. I also heard you say irrelevant, but this is now recorded and so let's get back to Mrs. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding certainly was that Mr. Zecevic would be about four hours, and my understanding was that Mr. Pantelic wasn't going to cross-examine at all because that was the last I heard. However, if Your Honours have allowed us three hours starting to -- Wednesday afternoon, then that leaves one hour for cross to begin by Mr. Zecevic and a further three hours on Thursday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Here is the situation. It seems that even if we use the three hours of examination-in-chief announced by the Prosecution, and if we take the full time announced by Mr. Zecevic and the one and a half hours announced by Mr. Pantelic, there is simply no way in which this entire thing can be achieved in eight hours, which is two days of his presence. There are a couple of options. One is that you could seek to shorten your examination-in-chief. The other option is that we could perhaps, if the schedule so permits, start earlier on Thursday, but that does depend a bit on -- Wednesday, sorry. That does depend a bit on -- on another trial not sitting on that day. So we could actually add an hour or two if we start earlier on Wednesday, but these are the options.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have worked on the basis that up till now we've had no rulings that the Sarajevo report was irrelevant. We have worked to ensure that Dr. Donia, in the three hours which you've permitted us to -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Sorry. You asked for three hours and we granted that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. That he would concentrate on the major documents which we consider to be relevant documents. If Your Honours rule after hearing argument tomorrow that everything in Dr. Donia's Sarajevo report, which is not specifically as such concerned with the siege of Sarajevo in terms that the general public understand, and, Your Honour, in this indictment there are three municipalities that relate to Sarajevo, and just to give Your Honours a foretaste, that is why we say it's relevant to this case, we will have to re-organise the documents in the manner in which they've been ordered, talk to Dr. Donia in order to cut out that -- those parts which we can't deal with, and in addition to that, I mean -- and basically speaking, all we'll have for that is the Wednesday morning, because I shall be opening tomorrow afternoon and arguing the -- the relevance of the Sarajevo documents. And so to start earlier is going to cause problems again. Your Honour, as I say, I don't know that we can stop him now, but it seems to me that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Korner, listen. What I don't understand is that even if we had proceeded on the avenue which was originally lined out, namely that he would be examined in chief and cross-examined on anything except the Sarajevo report and then to be called back later for the Defence teams to complete their cross-examination on the basis of that last report, even if we had done that there still would be insufficient time for you to complete what you had set out to do in two days of testimony. That's what I don't understand. So can you --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding was -- and I can't at the moment because I wasn't expecting, I'm afraid, this, and I did mean in parenthesis to ask for legal officers if matters were going to be raised so we could have advance notice, that, though, Your Honours said in open court, I believe at the Status Conference or somewhere in writing, we have something to the effect that Dr. Donia would finish at 12.00 and that, as he had to come back, any further cross-examination could take place then. Now, at the moment, of course, I can't lay my hands on that, because that's my understanding, and that's why we arranged for Dr. Donia to start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But that was under the assumption that the Defence teams might all together ask for leave not to -- to begin their cross-examination. But -- but since we are -- since we all along operated under the assumption that the Defence teams would be entitled and indeed expected to begin their cross-examination on the reports of Dr. Donia on the basis of the reports except the Sarajevo report, it just seems that you have walked on a very thin line here by -- by knowing that he would have to go back Thursday, and if indeed there is a plane that he can still catch Thursday after the hearing at 7.00, which I don't know if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. It may be that I've gone mad and it maybe it's late in the day and I've been on my feet all day, but my understanding was we raised, and if it wasn't with Your Honours, I thought we raised this at the Pre-Trial Conference, was that he had to go back on Thursday, lunchtime at the latest, to meet his professional commitment in the United States on Friday and that therefore we would sit in the morning. And if it wasn't in front of Your Honours it may be this was all being done internally by correspondence with the legal officers. I simply can't remember at the moment. But one way or another, Your Honour, we have worked on the basis that because cross-examination was going to be adjourned in any event, that Dr. Donia would do his evidence in chief, cross-examination would take place and if it couldn't be completed by Thursday lunchtime, then it would be adjourned until he came back. And, Your Honour, I'm really sorry. As I say, I wasn't expecting this discussion to take exactly this form. I imagined it was going to be a discussion about our application to add these documents, not as to how the testimony was going to work. I can, if I look for it, I'm sure find the various administrative matters. But the reality is, Your Honour, is this: If Your Honours are taking the view that cross-examination on the -- on the earlier reports must be completed by the time Dr. Donia leaves on Thursday, well, then you're right. At the moment I don't see that it's going to work. And therefore, the position is this: That we would like to put Dr. Donia off. We have no other evidence we can call this week, but as we're adjourning on Thursday in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Let's not panic, and I'm sure we will find a workable solution, but allow me to consult with my two colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mrs. Korner, can I just ask, and I understand your foot is hurting, if you want to sit down you're permitted to.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Have you arranged with CMSS that we could sit Thursday morning, because this is not clear to me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We understand that the Popovic case will be finished by then, and we can then use the court in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Can we ask the Registrar to confirm this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm informed by the Registrar that it is indeed a deal that we can sit in this trial Thursday morning, and also that if Popovic adjourns tomorrow, there might be a chance that the Popovic trial will not need a courtroom Wednesday morning, in which case we could begin earlier to save an extra couple of hours. Can I ask the Registrar to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
